Your committee recommend that, commencing with this session, the printing of both the English and French Revised Editions of the Debates for distribution to the public and the press be discontinued and that [DOT] the King's Printer be authorized to have printed during the course of the session for the use. of senators and members of the House 600 copies of the current sheets of the English Revised Edition and 100 copies of the French Revised Edition.
Mr. GERVAIS moved the adoption of the report.
Mr.'SPROULE. We have not had an opportunity of examining that report yet.

I would like to suggest to the hon. gentleman who proposes the motion, that I think he ought to make provision for the distribution daily of the unrevised edition of the 1 Hansard ' to the press and especially to the daily press.
That is provided for.
Does it cover that?

Yes, that is provided for in the regulations. As a matter of fact this report is merely to save a few dollars to the exchequer of Canada by discontinuing the useless distribution of a few thousand copies of the revised edition. The unrevised edition is distributed daily to the press and to the general public. I think that the press and especially my hon. friend (Mr. W. F. Maclean) will be satisfied. During last session every one was satisfied with this arrangement. This motion is

really to confirm that practice and to comply with the request made by the King's Printer.

We have been in the habit of issuing to the weekly and daily press a revised copy of the ' Hansard.' We decided there was no use in sending that out, that we would send the unrevised edition instead, and this is merely to authorize the King's Printer not to send out both the revised and the unrevised to the press generally. Mr. LEWIS moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 47) to provide for inspection of vessels not now inspected.
Explain.

Mr. Speaker, the object of the Bill which I now ask permission to introduce is two-fold. In the first place, clauses 1, 2, 3 and 4 refer to barges and vessels not now inspected. I know for a fact, Sir, that what I am about to say with reference to this matter is absolutely correct as far as the great lakes are concerned, and I am informed that the same conditions .exist in the maritime provinces. The custom is for old wooden boats and vessels, out of which the engines and masts have been taken, to be towed by other boats. While the government of Canada does not allow well found boats to leave a harbour unless they are properly equipped, no such provision for the safety of the crew is enforced in reference to these barges. One section of this Bill provides that they shall be inspected. Another section refers to steam yachts under five tons, clause 6 refers to fishing boats. These boats under a certain tonnage are not obliged to carry either a life boat, life raft or other apparatus for the saving of human life. In 120 Ontario reports, Sturgeon vs. The Port Bur-Mr. GBR VAIS.
well Fishing Company, page 154, it is clearly laid down in the judgment that had the boat in question, which is of the class referred to in this Bill, been equipped with life-saving apparatus, the lives of one or two men lost on that occasion would have been saved.
The last section refers to steamships towing vessels of steel which have not motive power. As is well known, these steel vessels cannot approach close to one another and the consequence is that when a line breaks, as frequently happens, the men on the tow are almost invariably lost. I desire by this amendment to provide that all steamships towing other boats shall have on board a rocket gun by which a heaving line can be sent 300 or 400 feet and a vessel with motive power can thus pick up her derelict tow. The United States steel trust which owns the largest number of vessels on the continent obliges all its vessels to carry rocket guns.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

CURRIE (North Simcoe) moved for leave to introduce a Bill to amend the Inspection and Sales Act. He said: I find that under the British North America Act, this parliament has exclusive jurisdiction in matters relating to weights and measures. This parliament in its wisdom has seen fit to pass legislation fixing standards for weights and other measures. Parliament has also passed an Inspection and Sales Act which deals with the standard weight of certain articles, such as a bushel of grain, a barrel of flour, a barrel of salt, a load of hay and a bag of potatoes in Quebec. Parliament has also fixed the weight of a dozen of eggs at one and a half pounds. I find, however, that the most important article of food entering into every-day consumption, that is the loaf of bread, has not been standardized by this parliament and the various municipalities and provinces have from time to time been struggling with this question, some of them endeavouring to fix the weight at one figure and others at another. Thus there is confusion and the law is not carried out. In consequence the public, especially the poorer classes, have suffered. I think that we should follow the wise legislation of the mother country and the other colonies in this respect and fix the weight of a loaf of bread as clearly as we have the right to do under the British North America Act.
This Bill is intended as an amendment and to become part 11 of the Inspection and Sales Act. The first clause defines the terms ' baker ' ' inspector ' and ' officers.'

The second clause provides that all bread sold by bakers shall be in loaves of one two and four pounds. That fixes a standard for the whole of Canada. Provision is made in the Bill for the carrying out of its provisions. It provides that inspectors under the Inspection and Sales Act, inspectors appointed under the Inland Revenue Act or other inspectors appointed by this government for special purposes, shall be considered inspectors under this part of this Bill. It also provides that the officials appointed under provincial statute or under municipal by-law, whose duty it would be to see to the enforcement of this Act, shall have jurisdiction in certain cases. Penalties are fixed for having bread under weight and also against a baker if he or the man who delivers his bread does not supply himself with proper scales and appliances to weigh the bread he is selling. I trust that the Minister of Inland Revenue, under whose care I presume this Bill will come, will expedite its passage through the House. I ask the indulgence of the House in reference to it because I think it is a measure in the interests of the public. It is an absolute necessity that we should have a standard weight for a loaf of bread and that standard should be so fixe'd that there will be some legal redress in case of a baker breaking the law.

There is a question as to whether a Bill of this kind should not be introduced by resolution. It seems to me to affect and regulate trade, which, under the general rule of the House, is a subject matter that must be introduced by resolution. If we are going to regulate the weight of a loaf of bread that regulates the trade in bread as much as any possible treatment of that trade can. It is well understood that Bills of that kind must be introduced by resolution.
If that be the fact, the minister must be a great offender, because he has introduced such measures without resolution.
I think my hon. friend will find that I have invariably introduced such Bills by resolution.
Perhaps not this session, but I think last session and the year before he did.
The hon. gentleman is entirely mistaken.
Has it not sometimes been the practice to have the Bills introduced and the resolutions brought in afterwards.

That has been done, I am merely drawing attention to the fact.
17J
It is quite proper that attention should be drawn to it, but I think that practice has been followed. Whether it be a correct practice or not I do not know.
It is against rule 48.

Rule 48 reads:
No Bill relating to trade, or the alteration of the laws concerning trade, is to be brought into this House, until the. proposition shall have been first considered in a Committee of the Whole House, and agreed unto by the House.
If it is a Bill in restraint of trade it will have to be preceded by a resolution, unless the House consents to the introduction of the Bill with the understanding that a resolution will be introduced later.
There is no objection to that.

I do not wish to cause any misunderstanding. The measure is not a measure in restraint of trade in any way, and the Bill provides clearly that there shall be no charges against the consolidated revenue fund by any of its provisions. I could quite understand that in the measure contained a clause whereby there was to be any charge against the\ revenues of this country it would be necessary to introduce it by a resolution. As far as restraining or regulating trade is concerned, it fixes the weight of a certain article. I would like to know from the minister if, when the weight of a barrel of apples was fixed by this House, that legislation was initiated by a resolution of the House.

I cannot say, but I think it was. Certainly if it was not it was contrary to the rules of the House. Bourinot says:
Rule 41 of the Rules of the House provides that no Bill relating to trade or an alteration of the laws concerning trade is to be brought into the House until the proposition has been considered in a Committee of the Whole House.
Then, later on it says:
Both in the English and Canadian Commons the rule, just cited, has been held to apply to trade generally, as well as to any particular trade, if directly affected by a Bill. It has also been decided that to bring a Bill under the rule it should properly propose to regulate trade as a subject-matter.
Under these circumstances, it seems to me that the Bill ought to be preceded by a resolution. I am not taking this objection for the purpose of blocking the Bill, but simply for the purpose of having it proceeded with regularly. The hon. leader of the opposition is quite right in saying that Bills have been introduced, probably on

several occasions, which, it has been afterwards found ought to have been .preceded by a resolution, and then the resolution has been proposed and put through the committee, and afterwards the Bill proceeded with.

Of course, I do not need to argue that two wrongs make a right; but if the hon. member for North Simooe is wrong on this occasion, the Minister of Agriculture was wrong yesterday. He introduced a Bill, and in the latter part of his explanation said:
The last clause defines the weight of a barrel of potatoes when potatoes are sold by the barrel.
I am quite sure that Bill was not preceded by a resolution.
My hon. friend is quite right. My explanation is that I referred the matter to the law clerk of the House of Commons, and he informed me that that Bill did not require to be preceded by a resolution.
Then plainly the one before the House now does not require a resolution, because both Bills are of exactly the same character.

Of course, it is for the House to say whether the rules are to he observed or not. Strict adherence to the rules is always advisable, and if I have to rule on the question of this Bill, my ruling will be that it will have to be preceded by a resolution.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is always preferable to conform to the rule, and it may be that my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture will have to revise his own Bill and have it preceded by a resolution. But I would observe that the Bill of the hon. member for North Simooe seems to be objectionable in another respect, not on its merits, but as being under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provincial legislature. The weight of bread is generally regulated by municipal authority, and it is^ very questionable if we have jurisdiction in the matter.
What about a barrel of. potatoes?	'

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The same thing would apply.
I think the Bill had better stand in the meantime until the matter is looked into further.
What aTe we going to do about the one of yesterday?

I may have been in error in allowing the Bill of yesterday to be Mr. FISHER.
introduced without being preceded by a resolution.

What is the reason that sometimes resolutions of this kind are dealt with by way of notice that proceedings will be taken on the following day, and sometimes the House is moved into committee at once? No, I think not. If they are proceeded with at once, it is simply by consent of the House. I will give notice that I will take it up on Monday.

In the case of a money Bill, notice should be given in advance, and then it becomes an order of the day. When it is a notice concerning a question affecting trade, it does not go on the Order Paper, and may be taken up at once.

In Bourinot.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No. I think in order to guard the rights of the people over money Bills, they must be preceded by a notice in advance. That is the reason of the rule.
This particular motion involves the payment of license fees.

I give notice that I will take it up on Monday next.

I would like to ask the right hon. the Prime Minister with reference to the International Congress on Alcoholism which was held last July in London, England. Sir WILFRID' LAURIER. I would have to refresh my memory on this point. I have no objection to bringing down the papers.

Would it not be possible to have the returns brought down in better shape? I mentioned this matter a couple of sessions ago. The grievance is a very frequent occurrence. I refer in particular to the papers brought down in connection with the resignation of Mr. Lumsden. They were not only up side down but inside out. They began at the end but did not end at the beginning. They were in such bad shape that it was impossible to ascertain where to look for any particular document. Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair, I desire to call the attention of the House to a doctrine laid down by the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) recently in dealing with a question which I had placed on the Order Paper in pursuance of the privilege conferred by rule of this House that members may, on due notice given, ask questions relating to public affairs. Sir, the question which I put related to the public affairs of this country, inasmuch as it referred to an appointment which is not exceeded in importance by any other appointment in the gift of the Dominion government, the office of Lieutenant Governor of British Columbia. We had an intimation through the newspapers that a political organization in British Columbia had by formal resolution passed, made a recommendation to the government at Ottawa that a certain gentleman should be appointed Lieutenant Governor of that province. This recommendation was made in the most public manner as a notification to other persons concerned to 'keep off the grass.' It was a notification that the British Columbia executive of the Liberal party having made such a recommendation, it was idle for any one else to butt in on that preserve, and that all should govern themselves accordingly. To my mind, that was a most shocking interfer-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
ence on the part of a political organization in the appointment to an office which should be non-political, should be kept strictly apart from all political considerations. I had hoped, when I saw that intimation in the press, that, upon receipt of that recommendation at Ottawa, the Prime Minister, if it came to his notice- as I suppose it would come to his notice as the man most concerned in the appointment-would administer to the committee in British Columbia the snub which their course deserved, would have informed them that, with respect to the office of Lieutenant Governor of British Columbia, they were exceeding their jurisdiction, they were violating the laws of propriety, in making any recommendation of that kind, particularly in making it in the public and theatrical manner in which they did make it. In pursuance of that idea, I placed a question on the Order Paper in the hope that the Prime Minister in answering it would have clearly laid down the principle I have indicated, and that his answer to that committee in British Columbia would have been a warning to political associations everywhere that here was an office upon which they must not lay their hands. I may say frankly that I was disappointed when I received the reply from the Prime Minister that,
Information of the description asked for in the first part of his question would be considered by the government or by any minister as absolutely private matter.
Sir, I must dissent from the doctrine that a recommendation on tne part of a public association such as the association I have described can properly be considered by the government of this country a private matter. To my mind it is an essentially public matter, a matter as to *which we are entitled to have the most complete information. To my mind, we are entitled to know what has been done with respect to that application. We would be entitled to it even under ordinary circumstances; but I claim that we are very specially entitled to that information in view of the very special circumstances respecting the gentleman recommended by this resolution for the Lieutenant Governorship of British Columbia.
We have observed toy the press that an election has been in progress in British Columbia. We have observed that one of the candidates in that election is the very gentleman whose application for the appointment of Lieutenant Governor has been favoured by the chief political association in the province. We find that gentleman, with this appointment as good as in his pocket-unless the government had turned down the recommendation in the manner in which I thought it should have been

turned down; unless the government consider that the publication of the recommendation of the patronage committee was absolutely fatal to the claim of the gentleman to whom I have referred-I say we have this gentleman, with the appointment of the Lieutenant Governorship of British Columbia as good as in his pocket, campaigning in that province against that very government on which he expected to sit in judgment as soon as that appointment was made. I invite the attention of this House to the condition these facts indicate, to the intolerable condition so far as the provincial government is concerned-that a man should toe one day on the hustings making most scandalous charges against the provincial government and the next day be called to the office of Lieutenant Governor. I do not wish to go into details, because this is a question of principle which I do not wish to befog with a cloud of words. But I wish to indicate the nature of the charges which this Lieutenant Governor designate has been making against the government of British Columbia, charges so grave that thejrhave Ibeen made the subject of an editorial in the chief Liberal organ of Canada, the Toronto ' Globe.' We read in the Toronto ' Globe ' the following:
The British Columbia election campaign has brought out the startling news that Premier McBride issued a secret order in council directing the sale of 3,238 acres of land in the Okanagan Indian reserve to a political favourite. The price at which this alleged sale was effected was $2.50 per acre, and as similar lands are sold in the neighbourhood for $300 and $400 per acre the fraudulent nature of the transaction is obvious. .	.	[DOT] The disclosure was made by Mr. Wade, K.C., in a campaign speech at Nelson, and it has not only startled the province, but has caused an uneasy feeling throughout the Dominion.
Here, Sir, we have, as the ' Globe ' sums it up in referring to the incident, a charge by the man who, so far' as we know, it is proposed to make Lieutenant Governor of the province-because, when the government had an opportunity to deny it they did not deny it, but said it was their private affair-that the McBride government has made a fraudulent sale of the public lands. Before referring to the bearing of that charge upon the question I am discussing, I might say, in justice tojthe McBride government, against whom charges of fraud do not lie and never have, that this allegation of this Lieutenant Governor designate is purely gratuitous, since the provincial government has no power to sell the lands referred to. So far as this alleged agreement of sale is concerned, it was merely an agreement between the provincial government and a gentleman who was applying to the Dominion government for
the sale to him of these lands, that, provided he could obtain the lands from the Dominion government having paid to them whatever price they saw fit to declare, the reversionary interest of the province of British Columbia in these Indian lands would be conveyed to him on the payment of the sum stipulated in this bargain. But we have this gentleman on the stump making a charge of deliberate fraud -a charge certainly so understood by the public and by the chief Liberal organ in Canada, and spread broadcast over the whole Dominion.
I think we are entitled to a pronouncement from the government on that question, an assurance that no man who has so stultified himself shall be considered to be eligible for appointment to the office of Lieutenant Governor, that our provincial governments may be protected from the insult to which they would be exposed by such appointments. I believe that we are entitled to have it laid down and clearly understood by the government and by ail applicants for office, that public office^ is not to be given as a reward for participation in a. political campaign, that we should have it made clear in British Columbia that these expedients will not be resorted to when it is impossible to get candidates to appear voluntarily against a government such as that of Mr. McBride, which has the confidence of the whole people of British Columbia-I believe there was one Liberal elected, a despatch apneared this morning in the newspapers, indicating that three Liberals had been elected, but I am told that the Minister of Inland Revenue, who represents British Columbia in the government, has subsequent returns which bring down the number of Liberals elected in British Columbia to one, or at the most two. So I say we are entitled to have from the government some assurance that possible candidates will not be induced to enter the field of politics by promises of appointment such as lieutenant governor-shios, or. positions on the Supreme Court and appeal court benches of British Columbia. I refer to the Appeal Court bench more particularly because of information which I gather from the newspapers, that a very serious wrong has been perpetrated there because of the holding up of the appointment of judges to the Appeal Court I'euoh until after the election which was decided yesterday when the gentlemen who were in the field as candidates would be released from the embarrassment of that position.	I find that a
man is imprisoned in the district of New Westminister, consigned to prison by a county court judge there conditionally upon the appeal court answering certain questions referred to them in a certain way. I find it stated in the press

that the judgment intimated that the Appeal Court was meeting on November 2, and therefore no hardship was involved by this peculiar sentencing, pending an appeal to that court. This unfortunate man is now appealing to the county court for a rehearing on the ground that there is no appeal court to which his case can be referred and in the meanwhile he languishes in prison while the bench of British Columbia is being made a football for what appears to be the political convenience of the persons who have the appointment of these appellate court judges. I think that this in'cident of the lieutenant governorship and of the withholding of the appointment of judges is a scandal. That it is so regarded by the people of British Columbia was made evident yesterday in no uncertain way. By their vote they showed the opinion they hold respecting the action of this government in these transactions, and I believe that as one of the representatives of British Columbia in this House it is my duty to call the attention of the government to these facts, as possibly otherwise they might fail to recognize the voice of the people expressed at the polls yesterday, as indicating to them the state of public sentiment in British Columbia with respect to our treatment by the government at Ottawa, in their manipulation of offices such as that of lieutenant governor and Appeal Court judge. I would like to have it brought out here that even if this thing has occurred, even if, for diplomatic reasons, the government do not like to admit having received the recommendation I have indicated, and do not like to indicate whether or not they have made a promise to these particular gentleman, we shall receive an assurance that nothing else of this nature will be tolerated.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
On a previous occasion my hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. J. D. Taylor) put the following questions to the government:
1- Has the government or any member thereof received from the executive of the Liberal Association for British Columbia, or any other political organization, any recommendation purporting to be made by resolution of that body, in favour of the appointment of I. C. Wade, Iv.C., as Lieutenant Governor of British Columbia? If so, what reply has been made?
2. Is the office of Lieutenant Governor one as to_ which the jurisdiction of patronage committee is recognized?
I have no objection to admit that we are responsible for, any action which we may take. At an early date we shall have to make the appointment of Lieutenant Governor for British Columbia because we Mr. J. D. TAYLOR.
have been notified by the present incumbent of the office that he does not intend to occupy the position beyond a certain date, and when that date arrives, it will be our duty to make an appointment and then we shall be open to censure or approval upon the recommendation we shall make to His Excellency, the Governor General. If at that time the selection which we make is not satisfactory to my hon. friend or to any member of the House we shall be open to criticism, but I think it would be fair of my hon. friend to wait until we have taken action before he criticises us.
.My hon. friend tells me we should have rebuked the gentleman who presumed to advise us to appoint Mr. Wade if any person did presume to give such advice. ' I do not know but there may be some merit in the suggestion of my hon. friend that we should rebuke any such attempt whenever it comes, but if we are to rebuke every one who offers us advice that we should appoint Mr. Wade, what are we to say to or how shall we treat that gentleman who says we should not appoint Mr. Wade? Does my hon. friend see any difference at all between the one advice and the other? If somebody from British Columbia says Mr. Wade is a fit and proper person to be Lieutenant Governor of British Columbia and if this be, in the eyes of my hon. friend an offence, how should we characterize the condjict of the gentleman who tells us that Mr. Wade is not a fit and proper person to be Lieutenant Governor of British Columbia? I fail to see why if it is wrong in one case it can be right in the other. I have to say to my hon. friend that it will be our duty to canvass the condition of th'ngs and try to make the best appointment possible in British Columbia. I go further. I have no hesitation in saying that the appointment which we shall make in British Columbia will be unimpeachable even in the very particular eyes of my hon. friend. As to the advice which is. offered to us, we are liable to receive advice from all quarters and from everybody. This Is a free country. It is the privilege of any body to offer advice whether it is proper or improper, but we receive such advice wherever it comes from. If it comes publicly we receive it, if it comes privately we receive it also, but I dissent altogether from the view advanced by my hon. friend that if any one chooses to write to us with a recommendation to make an appointment whether to the position of a messenger or any other position, that is a thing to be disclosed to parliament. I refuse to accede to that position and this has always been our attitude. We are liable only for the action we take. It cannot be seriously contended that we must be responsible for the letters tendered to us, on this or that question, above all on questions of appointments which are sent to the ministers for their guidance. I

have no hesitation in saying to my hon. friend that sometimes advice is offered to us in matters on which I think we should not receive any, and as to which we should be competent to discharge our duties, but we should not canvass these things too critically and too minutely. I have only to say that we must be judged in these matters by the result and by our actions and the time will come before many days are over when we shall have to take action. Then I shall invite the criticism of my hon. friend.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out, in very briefly replying to the right hon. the First Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), that this question is rather more important in its bearings as to the people at large in this country than he seems to imagine, and before saying another word I would 'also like to point out that the hon. member for NewWestminster (Mr. Taylor) did not specially offer the government any advice as to the appointment or non-appointment of Mr. Wade, but he rather indicated a line upon which Mr. Wade's appointment in this case would not be in the interest of the community at large because he would necessarily be a partisan after his indulgence in the political contest prior to the provincial election. Any man who had participated in the way he had done in this contest would necessarily put himself^ out of the pale of strict impartiality, which quality is so desirable in the occupant of the distinguished position of Lieutenant Governor. I also want to say one word upon this for the reason that this whole matter was discussed in connection with the appeal court the other day, and as it has a distinct bearing upon this question, I have to make some extended explanation touching upon this debate to-day. Referring ^ to the delay on the part of the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) in filling up the appointments to the new Court of Appeal of British Columbia, I made a statement regretting that those whose names were being bandied about by the press and the people of British Columbia as being likely appointees to the bench had unfortunately dipped strongly into the partisan politics of the day and, in saying that, I made this remark:
So far has it gone that some time ago despatches were published in the chief Liberal newspapers announcing that the late leader of the Liberal opposition in British Columbia, a gentleman who has the unfailing respect of all people in British Columbia, Liberals and Conservatives, and that gentleman and his friends seem to have attached such full credence to that report that he retired from the leadership of the Liberal party in British Columbia and, to his credit, is not taking any part in the campaign now in progress.
I would like to add that, while I do not take anything from my words in regard to the respect in which that gentleman, the late leader of the opposition, is held in British Columbia, it is my firm impression that much as he might have regretted dipping into the campaign, he was forced by the exigencies of party pressure to take part in it because it is very singular that on the very day on which I made that reference in this House, November 12, I have a report that:
J. A. Macdonald was the last speaker of the evening.
I am referring now to the gentleman who is to be made chief justice of the new court of appeal according to the despatches which have been printed. The report is of a meeting at Rossland:
He devoted his time principally to throwing cold water on the McBride railway policy.
Not very effectually, Mr. Speaker, as, of course, you can see. The point is of the greatest importance, and I think not only that my hon. friend from New Westminster is within his rights but that it is a timely thing to insist that, whether one party or another is in power in the Dominion or in a province, good government is impossible, and it will be impossible to fill high positions which should be above party, such as appointments to the judiciary and Lieutenant Governorships, if we have to wait and give these [appointments as political rewards to those who will work for their party to the eleventh hour and the fifty-ninth minute. That is the point that I want to make. I think it is a point that cannot be too strongly insisted on. The Minister of Justice, the other day, in his reply on this matter, stated that they would take their time, that it was not his delay or the delay of his department, and that he hoped to make the appointment from a list of gentlemen who were qualified to fill these positions on the court of appeal. Well, that may be true and while it is significant that the old Greeks represented justice as blindfolded because it was in the interest of no side or of no party and because justice should be dispensed evenly, it seems , that if the head of the department was blindfolded the bandage must have slipped a little down so that he could get a view of the situation as it occurred in that western province, and I am sure we will agree that his last view must have been extremely discouraging. I do hope that in the interest of good government all over the country the Prime Minister himself-and we recognized, I think, that he is not always driven by the exigencies of party politics, that he must clearly see how subversive it is of the best interests of the country-we will see less of these practices which have been followed of late in British Columbia and

that they will put these high offices so much above political partisanship that they will be entitled to the respect of every member of the community whether he be Liberal, Conservative, Socialist or Independent.

Mr. Speaker, I entirely agree with the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) that the government cannot be responsble for the tendering of advice, but that is an entirely different thing from what apparently goes on in practice. The government does become responsible when it recognizes the suggestions and recommendations of these patronage committees all over the country and if what comes to us from very authentic sources is to be regarded as accurate the patronage committee or executive committee, in British Columbia was only doing in this case what it has been doing right along and what other patronage committees have been doing right along, and in doing that they have received the recognition and endorsement of this government in many cases. I am speaking of it only from information gathered as to what I believe has actually taken place. The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Taylor) put forward a consideration which should appeal to the Prime Minister. How would it be possible to carry on government in this country decently when a man who has gone into an election campaign as a candidate and uttered the most serious charges against the provincial administration was doing that upon the promise or understanding after the election campaign should be over he should receive his reward in the office of Lieutenant Governor?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There was no such promise; not even hinted.

But that is the standpoint from which my hon. friend from New Westminster was arguing and he w'as pointing out to the Prime Minister that if anything of that kind had taken place conditions would he intolerable as I am sure the Prime Minister would himself consider them intolerable. Look at it for a moment. Suppose a Lieutenant Governor in this Dominion were to be selected in the person of some man who had been campaigning immediately before his appointment against the government who were to be his confidential advisers. The thing would be absurd, monstrous and ridiculous, and I am glad to have the assurance of the Prime Minister that there is absolutely nothing in the suggestion. But it does seem to me to be altogether another matter that he should dismiss so lightly the delay" in the appointment of the members of the court of appeal in British Columbia. I do not know of my own knowledge anything about the assertions which have been made by my hon. friend from New Westminster.

He has made them upon his own responsibility as a member of this House and, as I gather from his remarks, they are to the effect that a man is languishing in prison in British Columbia to-day because he cannot get his remedy under the law owing to this default on the part of the government and of the Minister of Justice. A more intolerable and a more disgraceful condition than that I cannot imagine. It is absolutely intolerable that the appointment of men to the court of appeal in British Columbia should have been delayed with such results as that. What was the answer the other day? The answer of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice was, forsooth, that the wheels of justice must stop because ne was away in Europe. The Act was proclaimed on the first day of September. He came back somewhere about the middle of October, I think, and he would not count the intervening six or eight weeks. Justice must stand still, the courts of British Columbia must remain without judges because he, on official duties, no doubt, had found it necessary or convenient to absent himself in the British Isles. When the Minister of Justice went from here in June or July last did he leave no other member of the government to preside over his department? Was there no other minister of the Crown, was there not the Prime Minister or some other member of the government, who could take up and who did take up the duties of that department? The excuse put forward by the Minister of Justice is absolutely unworthy of consideration. I say that within a week or ten days after that Act had been nroclaimed by the government of British Columbia the corresponding Dominion Act should have been proclaimed by this government and there should have been constituted a court of appeal in the province of British Columbia not later than the 20th of .September last, in which case the man who is now lving in prison because his rights under the law are denied him through the laches of this government would have been able to obtain his proper remedy under the law. Under these circumstances the country and the House ought to ask the Prime Minister and the government for some adequate explanation of the delay of now nearly three, months during which the machinery of justice in British Columbia has been absolutely out of gear.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance).
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am afraid, Mr. Speaker, that the leader of the opposition hardly gave a fair statement of what the Minister -of Justice said. I remember that the Minister of Justice said that he did not think the proceedings required such very great activity in the case of these British Columbia judges -because he pointed out that the government of British Columbia, after causing

the enactment of this measure, failed to proclaim it for very many months. And, curiously enough during that interim there was an election pending, and gentlemen on the other side are so ready to suggest that elections have something to do with things, might I mention that it was even rumoured that the reason why the British Columbia Act was not proclaimed was that the British Columbia government was waiting for the results of the Dominion elections in the hope that a Conservative government might have a chance to make the appointments.

May I ask a question?
Mr. FIELDING, Yes.
Is it not true that during the time the British Columbia government failed to proclaim their Act, there was an efficient and available court of appeal in existence?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I was merely pointing out that when the leader of the opposition undertook
Answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: One of my weaknesses is that I never undertake to answer a question when I am not familiar with the facts.
Or when you are in a tight place.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, I do not know that; I think hon. gentlemen opposite will give me credit for being ready to answer questions whenever I can. I was pointing out that the- leader of the opposition had hardly put the position of the Minister of Justice fairly, and I rose specially to take exception to some very dangerous doctrines that -were laid down 'by my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. Taylor). I took down the words of my hon. friend, and he says he wants this government to lay down as a principle that public office is not to he given to any one as a reward for service in a political campaign.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend says hear, hear, but I refuse to subscribe to that doctrine. The hon. gentleman himself holds an honourable and important office as a member of this House, and I have no doubt he received that office as a reward for his services in political campaigns. If my hon. friend did not get his office in that way, I should think he did not very well deserve it. In my opinion participation in political campaigns is not a crime. Politics is the business of the people at large, and the men who engage in politics, according to their respective views of public affairs, ought to 'be regarded as the best citizens in the country. It is the duty of every good citizen to participate in politics, and far from being a cause for condemnation, participation in political campaigns ought under proper conditions to be a cause for reward.
I hold a rather important office in the government of the country, and I venture to say that had I not taken a part in a good many political campaigns I would not have the pleasure of occupying it. This idea that a man is to be ignored and condemned because he takes a part in a political campaign is certainly a very strange notion. Then, my hon. friend from Yale (Mr. Burrell) went a little further; he said: Look at this question of the judgeships; here is the former leader of the opposition-a gentleman whom he spoke of and deservedly so in terms of respect-he actually went out and poured cold water on the McBride government and the hon. gentleman asked: Would you dare to make that man a judge after that? What a monstrous thing it would be to appoint a man to the bench after he has dared to pour cold waiter on a local government? Well, I have had a long experience along these lines. It was my pleasure and duty for a great many years to be the leader of a local government and I remember on one occasion that my chief opponent in the constituency of Halifax was a gentleman of the legal profession [DOT] and a very eminent one. He went out through the length and breadth of the province, he poured cold water and sometimes hot water upon the government which 1 had the honour to lead, and, fortunately,
I was successful and he failed. And, a very short time after that he was appointed by the Conservative government of the Dominion to the high and honourable position of Judge of the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia.
Was it not some years afterwards?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, it was not some years afterwards.
In what year was the campaign?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot tell my hon. friend, but I will remind him of the case.
I know the case.
Would the Minister of Finance permit me a brief explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

The only point I desired to make was in reference to the statement of the Minister of Justice, that he hoped to make the appointments at the end of the month, and that was why I said that sneaking on the 24th of No-, vember he only had six days in which to do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am referring to whether participation in a political campaign on one side or the other ought to be regarded as a disqualification for public office in this country, and I am dissenting most emphatically from the position taken by my hon. friend. Now, this gentleman to whom I referred was my opponent in the campaign in Halifax and very shortly afterwards-the leader of the opposition says several years, but I think he is is-taken in that; I am speaking from memory entirely, and I quite realize that memory may fail-very shortly afterwards; speaking now in good faith, a very few weeks afterwards that gentleman was appointed to the bench.
I do not think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will look it up as a
matter of curiosity, and if I am wrong I will tell my hon. friend.
Tell us all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would if I thought you were interested. At all events it is not important, for what I want to point out is that when this occurred it never seemed to any of us that there was any great wrong in appointing mat gentleman to public office. True, he poured cold water on that most excellent and virtuous government of which I was the leader.
Some hen. MEMBEES. Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As I have said, sometimes he made it rather hot for us. but when a short time afterwards he was appointed to the honourable position of a judge, far from finding any fault, when his professional associates-including the leader of the opposition-desired to do him honour, it was my pleasure and my privilege to preside at the dinner which was given to him on the occasion of his appointment.
Some hon. MEMBEES. Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And so I should think that my hon. friend ought not for a moment to lay down the doctrine that because a man has participated in a political campaign in any province of the Dominion it ought to be regarded as a cause of offence. From my point of view-always supposing he exercises his right as a good citizen properly and reasonably-I would say that instead of that being a reason why a man should not be appointed to a public office it may be a good reason why he should be honoured by such an appointment.

How does the Minister of Finance reconcile his statements to-dav with a resolution which was pass. ed in this House some years ago and voted on unanimouslv by the then Beform party, and which enunciated the solemn principle Mr. BURRELL.
that no man should be appointed to an office of emolument under the Crown during the time he was a member of this House or within two years afterwards?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If I had voted for any such resolution my hon. friend would make a good point, and I might not be able to square my views with that, but if the hon. gentleman will look up the records he will find that no such a resolution .was ever unanimously passed, and I do not think it was ever passed at all. At all events, speaking for myself, I never approved of it.

['If I had voted for any such resolution my hon. friend would make a good point, and I might not be able to square my views with that, but if the hon. gentleman will look up the records he will find that no such a resolution .was ever unanimously passed, and I do not think it was ever passed at all. At all events, speaking for myself, I never approved of it.']

This afternoon my hon. friend who represents Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) asked me if I would take up the items for public buildings in the province of Quebec. I told him I would try and do so. The hon. gentleman is not now in his place, and I do not know whether he is still desirous that I should take up the Quebec items. In the meantime, -with regard to the residence for the chief astronomer, which we were discussing when the House was last in committee, I stated that it was not intended to charge the chief astronomer any rental for the residence, following an example which was set by the Conservative government when the Experimental Farm was established. At that time a residence was erected for the director of the farm, Dr. Saunders, at a cost about the same as that of this building. The contract was for some $12,000 in addition to which there was the heating and lighting, just as in this case. The policy of the government then was not to charge the director of the Experimental Farm rent for the building, and the same policy was afterwards followed with regard to other residences erected in connection with the farm. I thought the same xiolicy would be adopted with regard to the residence for the chief astronomer. I may say, however, that since the matter was last under discussion before the committee, I have given further consideration to me subject and have conferred with the Minister of the Interior with regard to it, and we have come to the conclusion that as the chief astronomer, if he resided in the city of Ottawa, would be obliged to pay a rental for a dwelling house, it would not be unreasonable that he should pay for the residence near the observatory which the government is providing, such rental as he would have to pay for a suitable residence if he resided in the city of Ottawa.
$1,000 a year?
I am not prepared to say what a reasonable rental would be, as we have not conferred with Dr. King on the subject.
I asked the minister what would be a reasonable rental for this residence, and he said $1,000.

I said $1,000, but I am not in a position to say whether or not Dr. King would be prepared to pay that. Of course, it must be borne in mind that the government could afford to rent the house at a somewhat lower rental than a private individual, because the government pays no taxes on its property. Whether that would be $1,000 or not, I am not prepared to say at this moment, but it would approach that I should say.
An allowance is to be made to him for the house he is to occupy close to the observatory, not that you intend to rent a house for him in the city.
Oh, no. Ete would pay for the house we are constructing for him near the observatory.

The members of the committee will agree that some good result has come from the motion I made at the last sitting of this committee. At the time I had a conviction that the Minister of Justice had some purpose out of the ordinary in discussing the motion at the length he did in order to reach the hour of 6 o'clock. However, a regrettable feature of the repentance to which the Minister of Public Works has come in the interval is that he strikes home at-the innocent official instead of at his own department. I do not wish it to be understood that the purpose of this motion was in any way to affect Dr. King or the emolument that he receives. If the government were to go further and build a grander house still at the expense of the country, it would be no kindness to Dr. King. It would be just about as much unkindness to him as now to charge him $1,000 a year rental in order, if possible, to meet the wishes of the public in regard to the resolution which I have proposed. If they were to build a residence for him costing some $25,000 or $30,000, the doctor might have nothing left of his salary after he_ paid the expense of keeping it up. The principle I wanted to establish by the motion I made was this, that the government should adopt the rule of building for a salaried officer, if they built at all, such a house as the average man in this country would build for himself were he in receipt of the same salary. I do not wish to assent to the proposition that the government should undertake the construction of these residences at all; but this one is under construction, and I think a very good object would be served by cutting down the appropriation. It might serve the object of
having the residence built at a reasonable cost, because it will certainly be an exception if it is so built. Therefore, if the government has come to this late repentance in order to meet the public wishes by striking home at Dr. King, I think the better course would be to strike home at themselves and cut out $5,000 of the appropriation, and then they would have a house somewhat in excess of what a man in receipt of a salary of $3,000. usually occupies in Eastern Canada. I beg to renew the motion which I made at the last sitting of the committee, to the effect that $5,000 be struck off that appropriation, the same to apply to the residence to be built for the chief astronomer.

I feel that possibly I may have been responsible for some of this discussion. But when I referred to the matter, I had no desire to speak of this building particularly, but simply to draw the attention of the government to a few other buildings that they might have in contemplation. I do not agree for a moment to the suggestion of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) that Mr. King the chief astronomer, should pay a rental. I think he is punished sufficiently when he has to live in a house that costs $17,000, because it costs more to live in a house of that kind than in one which costs $8,000 or $9,000 which would be about the right amount for the residence of an official getting three or four thousand dollars a year. I would be sorry to see Mr. King punished to any greater extent than he is going to be, as it is. But I hope-in view of what I believe, namely, that the officials of the Public Works Department have been responsible for the extra cost of a lot of buildings -that they will be compelled to make their plans of a more moderate character. In my remarks I had no intention of singling out this building in particular but of dealing with the buildings in general. Take those erected for the officials of the Militia Department. There ought to be a general cutting down of the cost of such buildings. In this case the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) was perfectly satisfied to have a house of moderate cost, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) only wanted a house of reasonable cost, but the officials increased the cost. I have heard men say on this side that in the case of post offices and the like, it is almost impossible to get the officials to make plans that insure a perfectly suitable and less expensive building for certain places. I make this explanation because I do not want to be put in the position of hurting Mr. King in any way. If Mr. King has now to pay rent in addition to living and furnishing an expensive house, you are punishing him twice, and I should be sorry to be responsible in any way for that condition of things.

We on this side welcome the remarks of the hon. member for Assini-boia (Mr. Turriff) in condemnation of the party and the government of which he is a prominent supporter. But I take issue with my hon. friend on one point. I do not subscribe to the policy that a government can shift their responsibilities on to a paid official. If the government had done their duty in this case, the Minister of Public Works would have said to the chief architect: We want you to submit a plan for a building that will cost not more than six or seven thousand dollars without the lot. Does the hon. gentleman suggest that if the chief architect were so directed, ihe would bring in a plan for a building to cost, as this one did in the first instance, I am informed, more than $25,000?
Oh, no.
My hon. friend stated last year that when the chief architect submitted the plan for his consideration, he sent it back and asked him to reduce the amount.
I do not think he named $25,000.

Perhaps not, but I am sure the minister will not say that it would not have cost $25,000. Does he say that the first plan submitted would not cost that? He does not reply. I was quite sure he would not. Therefore it is not fair to condemn an official when the responsibility rests with the minister and the government themselves. I have sufficient respect for the chief architect of the Public Works Department to believe that if the minister had instructed him to submit a plan for a residence to cost not more than $6,000 or $7,000 he would not have submitted one to cost $17,000 or $18,000.

I desire to correct the impression under which some hon gentlemen are labouring, and that is that some injustice will be done the chief astronomer by providing him with a house of the character of the one which is being constructed. The plans were submitted to Dr. King and everything done in connection with this plan had his entire approval.
Was he told he would have to pay rent?

No, but that he would have to keep up the house and that the expense of so doing, outside the rent, would have to be borne by him. That is what my hon. friend (Mr. Turriff) referred to when he talked of the expense of keeping up a larger as compared with keeping up a smaller residence. Therefore no injustice could be done Dr. King except in requiring him to pay rent, if that be an injustice.
It is proposed to cut down the item $5,000 and the minister objects, but he wants to charge a rental for a $17,000 house. Would it not be a mercy to Mr. King to have the estimate reduced $5,000?

No, this is just the kind of house Dr. King wants. Indeed he asked for a house somewhat larger. My hon. friend (Mr. Blain) made the remark that if the chief architect had been directed to plan a house to cost $6,000, he would have done so. I do not think my hon. friend does justice to his knowledge of buildings when he suggests that it would be creditable to this country to erect at the public expense a residence for so prominent an official as the chief astronomer and to direct that it should not cost more than $6,-
000.	That would not be a suitable residence. You must bear in mind that this is not a brick cased residence. It is not a building with wooden partitions in the cellar, but the partitions are of brick. The house itself is a brick building, the joists are of iron or steel, the house is built as nearly fireproof as it is ordinarily possible to build a residence. The policy of the government in the construction of public buildings is to make them as nearly fire proof as possible and so substantial that the ordinary depreciation will be as light as possible. The cost of the building in question is substantially the same as that of the dwelling erected by the former. government for Dr. Saunders, director of the experimental farm.
How much is it?

The price paid to the contractor was about $12,000, which is about the contract for this residence. In addition, in the case of Dr. Saunders' residence, there were the heating and lighting and certain contingencies also to be nrovided for. And Dr. Saunders' house was built about twenty years ago, when the wages paid to workmen were not within fifty per cent of what they are to-day-and that I leave to the judgment of every member of this House who has hp/d any experience in building.
Is Dr. Saunders' house about the same size as this? I understood the minister to say this was a two-story house.
Two stories with an attic.
Is it the same size as the house built for Dr. Saunders years ago?

Dr. Saunders' house is a wooden house and ought not to be so expensive as the one we are now building for the chief astronomer; yet the contract price is practically the same. This is a brick house, a more substantial structure and in every way better than the one erect-

ed by the old government for Dr. Saunders, and, as I have said, was put under contract for practically the same amount. Now let me say a word to my hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) with regard to his motion to cut down this estimate. I submit to him that the time to have mov.ed such a motion was last session. At that time when this matter was before the Committee of Supply last session, I stated what was the contract price; I stated that we had called for tenders and that the lowest tender was $12,300. I informed the committee as to what would be the probable cost of the complete residence and asked for authority to proceed with the work. The committee voted the sum of $14,000, and upon that the contract was entered into. The country is; now under obligation to pay to the contractors $12,300; and if the committee were to act upon the suggestion of my hon. friend and reduce this vote we should have to break faith with the contractors. We cannot now alter the plans for the building; we cannot provide for aTiuilding at a lower cost, because the country has agreed to this building and to pay the contractor this price. I think my hon. friend will see upon reflection, that now is not the time for his motion, but that, the contract having been entered into and the building substantially completed, the contractors must be paid the amount of their contract.
The minister says that the contract price ior Dr. Saunders' house was about $12,000. Will he say that that contract did not include everything?
It did not; I say that on the authority ot the chief architect.
Will the minister (Mr. Pugsley) lay that contract on the table, that we may see what it did include? I am under the impression that it included everything except some minor fittings.
I will lay the contract on the table.

As the minister has made the comparison between the building erected some years ago and this one, I would like to know, for my own information, if the minister can state definitely what was the size of that house and what it cost. He says he thinks the contract was about $12,000. But, before I attempt to discuss the matter, I would like to know the exact facts. This comparing of indefinite sums is not very satisfactory.

I stated to the committee on a former occasion what this house will cost, but I will give it again. The total expenditure, which includes the printing and advertising, the heating and boilers, the electric wiring and fixtures, the sidewalks and fencing and the cost of superintendence, will be $17,041.49. Deduct $500 for fencing and sidewalks, and the cost of printing and advertising and you have about $16,400 as the cost of the building.
Without the land?
Yes,
Did the minister take into consideration the $11,000 or $12,000 of which he spoke on a former occasion?

Yes, that is all included. The total cost of the building alone is about. $16,400. I would say to my hon. friend from Souris (Mr. Schaffner) that, as to the cost of Dr. Saunders' residence, it would be better that I should lay the contract on the table, for so we shall have the exact facts before us. But the Chief Architect tells me that the contract price was about $12,000, and that did not include heating or lighting.
_ Mr. SCHAFFNER. What will the heating and lighting of this house cost?
About $2,500.

The minister has said that it would be a breach of faith to dissolve the contract for this building. It seems to me it is for the House to decide whether it would be a breach of faith with Dr. King to charge him rent for a building more expensive than he expected to have. I remember that when this matter came up last session it was opposed by every member on this side of the House. We thought that this was too expensive a house for an official enjoying the salary of Dr. King. Dr. King might readily agree to a reduction in the cost of the house if he knew that he was to be charged rent.
I did not say that it would be merely a breach of faith; it would be a breach of contract. The building is nearly completed and we shall have to pay the contractor.

I do not understand how the minister accounts for the $25,000 vote for this building. Last year, $14,000 was voted, and we are asked to vote $11,000 this year. The minister has stated the cost of the residence at $17,000 or less, and I under*-stand that two other buildings are being provided at a cost of about $6,000. There would seem to be nearly $3,000 unaccounted for.

Perhaps my hon. friend (Mr. Crocket) did not hear my explanation. The same question was asked by another hon. gentleman when the matter last came before the committee. It will be seen by the wording of this vote that it is not confined to this residence but covers 'Ottawa Astronomical Observatory-additional buildings, etc.' That is the way the vote has been carried on since we began the con-
Are those other items for the other building in addition to the $6,000?
Oh, yes.

I understood the minister to say that he considered $1,000 to be a reasonable rental for this House and that he would charge Dr. King the same rental as Dr. King would be likely to pay for a house in the city. Six per cent of the cost of this house, that is $17,000, would make a rental of $1,020. Does the minister think it would be fair to charge an official more than one-third of his salary for rent, and has Dr. King consented to pay more than one-third of his salary for rent?

The conclusion at which I have arrived, after considering the matter since we discussed the item the other day is that it would be fair that Dr. King should pay the same rental that he would be required to pay in the city foT a suitable residence for him. I do not know whether that would be $1,000 or a less amount. Of course, we must bear in mind that it would be fair to allow, in respect to government moneys invested in the building, say four per cent. That is the very highest the government pays for money. Then there are no taxes, but there would be a certain wear and tear each year. Possibly somewhere between $600 and $800 would be a reasonable rental for the government to charge. My idea is that he should pay such reasonable rental as he would have to pay for suitable accommodation in the city of Ottawa.

The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) has put it very pointedly to me that I should have introduced this resolution when the same subject was under discussion on the 4th of February last. During that discussion the viciousness of the whole undertaking was very thoroughly laid before the minister. Every opportunity was then given him for repentance both along the line of his present repentance, and on the broad principle of the transaction. The minister, however, having everything laid before him on that occasion did not see fit to reduce the esti-mite himself, or to come to the conclusion he came to last night to make the astronomer pay rent. Therefore, I retort on him, would it not have been far better for him then to have frankly told the House that they did not purpose making this gentleman pay rent. I find at page 619 of ' Han-Mr. PUGSLEY.
sard ' of last year that the question of having Dr. King pay some rent for the house was brought to the attention of the minister and he then frankly told the House that he did not purpose making Dr. King pay any rental at all.
The facts laid before the House by the minister on the 4th of February last were quite different from those laid before us now. On the 4th of February last, the dis-eussion proceeded all along the line of the ultimate cost of this residence being $15,-
000.	To-day it is $17,000. Is that not a reason
Is my hon. friend sure I said $15,000? Did I not say about $16,000?

In one place in the remarks of the minister he seems to have been misread by other members. The minister did say about $16,000, but further op he was asked if $15,000 was not the ultimate cost and the sainister did not dispute the figures. And furthermore throughout the discussion
That is very different. I did state $16,000.

But the point was put very direct to the minister at page 619 by Mr. Staples, who said;	.
Are we to understand that $15,000 will complete this residence? My experience is that these buildings cost twice their estimated cost.
That shows that the gentleman was a long way astray.
It shows also that the minister took advantage of the opportunity not to put him right.
That would be a very heavy contract generally.

There was the opportunity of his life then to put the far-astray member for Macdonald right, but this is his reply;
This contract is for the building alone, and then there will be the heating and wiring and I assume, from information I have, that $3,000 or $4,000 additional will be necessary.
That would make it $16,300.
But why did not the minister so state? It was one of the characteristic replies of the minister.
I supposed the hon. gentleman could add the two figures together.

Where were the other figures? The whole matter, may I inform the minister, is on a par with many others that came before this committee last ses-

sion. There was not an apportioning of the cost of the residence and the coelostat hut and other matters, but all were lumped in a single vote of $14,000. The same expedient is used this session. In the course of one of his remarks he used $16,000 and throughout the whole discussion $15,000 was used as the cost of the residence, and the minister, courteous as usual and more than courteous in this case, continued not to correct us in the impression that $15,000 was the limit. How much of this $11,000 that he asks for this session is to be applied to the residence and how much to the other buildings?

There is still due on the contract $8,320. Then we purpose spending an amount for heating boilers, estimated by the chief architect to be $1,500; electric wiring and fixtures, $1,000. We expect it will cost $500 for sidewalks and fencing, and that contingencies with superintendence will cost $1,700, and all this vote will be used for these purposes.
That amounts to the whole $11,000? Then I understand the whole $11,000 is to be applied to the residence.
To the residence.

But the minister told us last year that it would only take $3,000 or $4,000 to finish the residence. It is no wonder that we do not know where we are at. Furthermore, it seems to me that in arriving at a fair value of a house good enough for any servant of this government-
I assumed my hon. friend would understand that we have yet a part of the vote of $14,000 of last year to be used during the current year, which will not expire until March 31 next.

I understand that, but no man can understand how much of the vote of the year before last and of last year and of this year is being applied to this residence. The point which I wish to make is that the salary received by a civil servant is about all this committee has on which to judge as to the character and expense of a house that would be appropriate for him. Where was the minister on February 4 last when we asked what salary this man was getting? He *was absent, he could give no information at all. We were, on the 4th February last, absolutely in the dark as to what salary this man obtained, and, therefore, absolutely in the dark as to one of the main principles that should govern us in deciding how much should be provided for his residence. Therefore, there is ample reason for moving at a later stage for a diminution. If the fact that the minister 18
has entered into a contract is going to tie the hands of the committee, why submit it to the committee at all? It is before the committee for approval or disapproval. The circumstances have altered since last February. Facts are before us that were not before us then. We could vote in perfect honour and in justice to our constituents that a man should be given a house such as an ordinary citizen of this country might occupy performing like service, and receiving like, remuneration.

I would not trouble the committee were it not for the fact that my hon. friend has sought to convey the impression that there was some misstatement of fact to the committee when this matter was up last session. Before any hon. gentleman undertakes to make an insinuation of that kind with reference to a minister he should be absolutely sure of his facts.
I made no insinuation; I made an absolute statement.
The hon. gentleman said that I led the committee to believe that this building was going to cost $15,000.
That is not the statement I made.
The hon. gentleman made that statement unless there is something very defective in my memory.
I did not.

I know the hon. gentleman made the statement and, unless he says he did not-
Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER I must point out that where a member denies that he made a statement that denial must be accepted.

The statement that I made-
Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER I think it also extremely desirable that any decision of the chairman should be received in silence with neither approval nor disapproval.
What I said was that the discussion proceeded on the assumption that $15,000 would be the ultimate cost and that when the minister was questioned whether it would or would not be he did not deny it.

Let me read the first statement I made when the item came before the committee. The item was :
Ottawa Astronomical Observatory-additional buildings, &e., $14,000.
This is the explanation I made to the committee:
This vote of $14,000 is asked to make provision for the construction of a residence for the chief astronomer, and also to complete

Every one who listened to the reply of the Minister of Public Works must realize that it is in keeping with the manner in which he gets out of a very close corner. From the little experience I have had the minister has led me to believe that he is very apt to get out of any corner he has got into before the committee. The minister has stated that he did not lead the committee to believe that this building was going to cost $15,000. What the hon. member from Portage la Prairie did say was that the discussion was conducted freely during that debate on the assumption that the building was going to cost $15,000.
May I ask the hon. gentleman what warrant he has for that statement when I made the specific statement that it would cost $16,000?

Just because the Minister himself stated so. I will read his statement to him before I proceed further. The hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Staples) asked:
Are we to understand that $15,000 will complete this residence? My experience is that these buildings cost twice their estimated cost.
The Minister of Public Works said:
This contract is for the building alone and then there will be the heating and wiring, and I assume from the information I have that $3,000 or $4,000 additional will be necessary.
Add $4,000 to $12,300 and what does it make? 1 Mr. PUGSLEY.

The whole discussion proceeded along the same line and every one who asked a question did so under the belief that the building would cost $15,000. Later the Minister of Public Works said:
The lowest tender is a little over $12,000 and with the heating, wiring and plumbing it will likely cost somewhere between $15,000 and $10,000.
I do not think the minister has any right to assume or suggest that my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie has misquoted him or has tried to make it appear that he had endeavoured to lead the committee to believe that the building was only going to cost $15,000. The assumption last year was that that was the cost of the building and my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie made that quite plain.

The Minister of Public Works gives as a reason why this vote should pass that a residence was built by a previous government costing a similar amount of money. Admitting that for the sake of argument and believing as I do that every item of this kind and every change should be decided upon its merits, in order to make that a parallel on which to pass our judgment it will be necessary to have all the facts in connection therewith. While I do not pretend at this moment to have full knowledge of these facts I would like to know whether when the house was built for Dr. Saunders at the Experimental Farm it was not the case that his residence was understood to be a part of the emolument. It was thoroughly understood at that time that the building erected for the manager of the farm would be occupied by him free of cost. It was practically an official residence. His office, altogether likely, was situated in the building and probably part of the staff occupied quarters there. In any case he would there entertain a number of visitors who would require to go there from time to time on official business. So that the case the minister has cited is not parallel with the one we have here and for that reason I do not belive that any member of the committee should be asked to take that into consideration.
Amendment negatived. Yeas 42, nays, 67.
