speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The rule is that an hon. member cannot vote unless he has heard the question put.

Item agreed to.
New departmental buildings, Ottawa, $300,000.
['The rule is that an hon. member cannot vote unless he has heard the question put.']

The question of these new departmental buildings has been before parliament during the last few sessions and as last year and the year be-

fore I gave full explanations I do not sup^ pose it will be necessary for me to go into details now. This $300,000 is to make provision for the completion of the payments for the land and also to enable the department to ask for tenders and enter into the contract for the construction of the buildings.
Is that all the information the minister proposes to give?
Unless some questions are asked.
There will be questions asked.
I fully explained the matter last session.
This is the first vote for the construction and we would like to know what the proposed buildings are to cost, what their capacity and what use they will be put to.

The building will have one frontage on Sussex street and another on Major Hill park; length 590 feet and width 250 feet; two large courts 154 by 79; the building will have six stories and a basement on the park and seven stories and a basement on Sussex street; it will be 125 feet high on McKenzie avenue and 150 feet high above Sussex street; the centre of the building will face York Street which is quite a wide street. The lower end of the building will be 503 feet from St. Patrick street and the upper end 247 feet from the Lindsay property. It will be built of stone.
What kind of stone?

Something similar to that in the Museum. The floor areas will be substantially laid: ground and first floors 148,256 superficial feet, second, third, fourth, fifth and sixth floors, 360,110 superficial feet. The basement on Sussex street will have 51,080 superficial feet, the tower rooms 9,984 or a total area in superficial feet of 596,430 or a net office area of 350,000 superficial feet.
How many officials will it house?
It will be sufficient to house all of the clerks who are now accommodated in rented buildings or perhaps even more than that.
How many is that?
What we rent to-day is about 300,000 superficial feet and this is 500,000 superficial feet.
Will this do away with the necessity of renting offices?

We hope it will, but the business of the country is expanding so 184
rapidly that what may be our hope to-day in that respect may not be realized five years hence.
What is it to cost?
It is estimated that the cost will be $3,439,200.
What does that include?
This includes everything but furniture; it will include the building and the heating, and the lighting, incidentals, contingencies, everything which ordinarily forms part of a building.
The minister must be able to give the cost of the building itself and also the cost of the fittings.

I am afraid I cannot. The architect estimates upon the total cubic contents. The plans are not worked out sufficiently in detail so that I cannot tell just what the heating or lighting is going to cost.
The plans are not fully worked out?
No.
How do you get at the cost then?
An architect can estimate pretty well what a building will cost taking the cubic contents.
Does that include elevators?
Yes, it includes everything.
Everything but the furniture?
Everything but the furniture.
Is the site included?
No.
What is the cost of the site?
Up to the 21st of September, 1909 we have paid for properties $528,000 and they have all been purchased but two.
What was the last one purchased?
and F. B. Hayes and F. McDougall; that purchase was completed on the 14th of July.
Who were the purchasing agents?
Mr. Riopelle?
You had agents besides Mr. Riopelle?
No, we had valuators some time ago, but Mr. Riopelle has been the agent to make the purchases.
No one else has been associated with him?
Except as valuers.
Of any particular lot?
In the expropriation proceedings; also the solicitors.
Who are the solicitors?

Mr. A. W. FraseT and Mr. McLean. There aTe two properties still to 'be purchased. We have expropriated them, but have not paid the money. One lot is that of Mr. James Inglis, 100 feet by 150 feet 9 inches. For this w"e have made an offer of $38,000, which has not been accepted. Then the other is a half lot, 33 feet by 155 feet 9 inches, of Martha and Columbus Eagleson. For this we have made an offer of $7,750, which they have declined to accept.
That would make a total of about $575,000?

Adding together the three amounts I have mentioned, that would be the total cost of the land, assuming that our offers are accepted. It is estimated that buildings and land together -will cost a little over $4,000,000.

What is to be the inside style of these buildings? Are they to follow the style of the other departmental buildings, and have small offices with a few clerks in each, and a few larger rooms, as in the later buildings, or has the minister, and the architect under his direction, had occasion to look at other business buildings, and if they have, have they decided on some other plan of inside arrangement?
That has been considered, and provision will be made to meet the very idea my hon. friend puts forward.
Then the minister might give us an idea of what is proposed.

What we propose to do in the first instance is to have a number of large rooms, to be arranged in consultation with the different departments. We shall have to have, of course, a number of small rooms as well. These will be decided upon after consultation with the ministers whose officials are to be accommodated in the building. We shall have a great many more large rooms than aTe contained in the present buildings. We recognize the desirability of affording accommodation for many clerks in one room under the eye of the chief of a branch of that department. We have not the details worked out yet.
How near will the centre of the building come to the sojcalled Lindsay block?
About 247 feet.

This new building will
accommodate the Militia Department, the Census and Statistics Department, part of the Interior Department, the new' Naval Department, I presume, and what others?

All that are now in the rented buildings-the Department of External Affairs, the Department of Labour, the Civil Service Commission, the Inspectors of Penitentiaries

	[DOT]

The Transcontinental
Railway Commission and the Navy Department?
Yes.
How much is now paid in rentals for the offices that will be taken care of by this building?
About $140,000 a year.
For what length of term are the various leases?

For from three to five years. There are none longer than five years. We have made the leases so that we shall be able to get rid of the leased properties about the time we hope to have the new departmental buildings completed.
When does the minister expect that the proposed building will be completed? -
That is a pretty difficult question. It is a pretty large building. I should think that if wo got it completed in four years we would be doing pretty well.
As this is going to involve an expenditure of $4,000,000, that is, more than half the original cost of the parliament buildings, we should have more detailed information about this building.
The public buildings in Ottawa, I think, cost between $9,000,000 and $10,000,000.

I do not think we should vote any appropriation upon the estimate of an architect who has made his estimate solely on space. I think the House is entitled to further information as to the kind and size of this building, and the plans and specifications should be submitted to the House; because we shall probably have the same experience w'ith regard to this building that we have had with regard to others. After we have committed ourselves to the proposed building by voting this $300,000, we shall be charged with having assented to a great

many details that we shall probably object to later on. On such an expenditure we should have a great deal of information, probably all that the minister has and a great deal that he has not got yet.

I have given to-day, I think, pretty full information. I have given the size of the building, the height of the building, the materials out of which it is to be constructed. Surely my hon. friend does not expect me to go into all the details of the construction of the building. I think that would be very unreasonable.
Has the minister yet got a regular series of plans and specifications?
The plans are pretty well completed.
Does the minister think he should not submit these to the House?

I will be very glad, if the hon. member or any other member desires it, to lay the plans on the table; but I think he will see the unreasonableness of postponing this item until that is done. On concurrence I will have the plans laid on the table.
What does the minister propose to do with this appropriation?
Complete the plans and specifications, call for tenders for the building, and make a start by tearing down the old buildings and preparing the foundations of the new building as soon as possible.
The plan I have seen included a bridge across the Rideau canal. Is it the intention of the government to have such a bridge as well as the building?

That idea was thought of and a plan was prepared showing a bridge, but my own view is that we can get along quite a number of years without a bridge. The bridge would cost close on to a million dollars. There might be a small foot bridge.
Before passing this estimate we should have some complete statement of the government's estimates and the cost of the building to be erected on Sussex street.
I have given them.
Does the hon. gentleman include in his figures the cost of the removal of the buildings which have to be taken down before the new ones can be erected?

That is included. It will be provided in the specifications that the contractor shall remove the old buildings. In the large majority of cases, he will find the material he gets will equal, if not exceed, the cost of the removal. That will be included in the contract and is estimated for in these figures.
From what we have heard now, the new building when completed, is to cost a little over $4,000,000. That is practically the estimate for land and building.
Yes; of course not including fixing up the grounds after the building is completed.
I am speaking of the cost of the building and the site.
Yes.

Reference was made to the cost of the departmental buildings in Ottawa by way of comparison. I notice in the public accounts that the cost of the government buildings at Ottawa or their value is put down at $8,156,800. That I understand will include the cost of the buildings on the hill, the main building with the recent improvements, the library, the east and west wing and the Langevin block as well. It would also include no doubt the Printing Bureau, the Mint; and the Museum, which is now rapidly approaching completion would no doubt be included in the valuation of the government buildings in Ottawa up to the time these public accounts were prepared. Also the Archives, and there may be some other buildings which I have overlooked. I had always understood that the buildings on the hill including the Langevin block practically only cost about $5,000,000. But we have since then erected some pretty costly buildings. Tlje Museum is a costly building, and is now, I understand, _ rapidly approaching completion. The Mint is a costly building, and I trust now is nearly completed. As I have said, we have the Printing Bureau, the Archives and some others. So, no doubt the $8,156,800 is a correct valuation of all the public buildings in Ottawa, and what is proposed now, is to erect one building at a cost at any rate of half the value of all the public buildings we have in Ottawa at present. All I desire to. do is draw attention to this and have a distinct understanding of what the estimate of the minister is because he may expect to be held down to his estimate very closely by those who may be here in future years.

Would my hon. friend bear this in mind, that we are>
paying today for outside buildings 4 per cent on $3,500,000?

I am not criticising the propriety of erecting this new building because I understand that is a foregone conclusion. But when the previous vote

was taken, determining that a building should be erected, we had not such full details of the size and cost of the building as we have now, but in a few years no doubt, attention will be drawn to the statement made here to-day, and the minister may expect to be held down very closely to the estimate he has given. And I trust we shall not be called upon inside of the four years, in which it is thought this building will be completed, to expend more than one half the amount that the entire public buildings we now own in Ottawa actually did cost.

I do not think the minister should expect us to enter upon this expenditure of $4,000,000 or more without a little more discussion and a little more details with reference to the plans and what is proposed to be done. It is rather a startling statement to find in the public estimates that we are going to expend on one building about half as much as it has cost us to construct all the government buildings we have. It is all very well to say you are going to keep within that estimate, but what we particularly want to know, is wheuier that is an extravagant estimate or not. How did the minister arrive at that estimate? What skill, if any, outside his departmental officers, did he have? Then a very important inquiry would be as to what is the space provided by the government buildings which are now erected and which have been built for about $8,000,000, and how does that compare with the space to be provided by this building. We want to find out whether this is an extravagant estimate or not and whether it is not possible to erect a building for our accommodation at a less cost than $4,000,-
000.	We must take into account the fact that wages have increased and some kinds of building materials cost more as well, but the main thing to be used is stone, and the cost of the stone itself would not be very much increased. But we are asked to sanction an expenditure, to give the minister an initial vote upon which a hard and fast contract may be given before we meet again, and we are entitled to have a look at the plans and see whether or not there are any suggestions to be made. We want to have a thorough explanation of these plans and what they provide for from- the minister himself. It is rather absurd that we should spend only fifteen minutes authorising an expenditure of $4,000,000 about which we have never seen the plans and know very little. It may be that some of us will not know much more after seeing the plans, but it is still better that we should have a look at them and have an explanation.

I think the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) is only-reasonable. I should he glad to have the Mr. HENDERSON.
plans brought here and give all in detail that it is possible to give. Perhaps it might be better to let this item stand, and, this evening, take up items with regard to which there might not be the same
Don't forget the floor-space.

I might just say that the Langevin block contains 90,000 superficial feet of floor-space, and cost $1,250,000. The whole three blocks of departmental buildings contain 315,000 superficial feet. Therefore, we shall have nearly fifty per cent more space than is contained in all three of the present departmental buildings.
I do not think the minister has given us the floor-space of the buildings covered by this amount of $8,000,000.
No.
Would there he any objection to allowing us to look at the plans not accepted, but for which a certain amount of money was paid as prize-money?

Not at all. They were all here last year in the Railway Committee room. I may say we could hardly display them in the Chamber. They are on file in the department, and the chief architect will he glad to show them to any hon. member who would like to examine them.
It would not be too much trouble to have the plans that have been accepted hung in the Railway Committee room for the information of members?

These buildings are not 'being constructed upon any plan accepted from outside. The plans on which it is proposed to proceed with construction are prepared by the chief architect of the department. We could have these brought in.
Does the minister say that the plans are completed?

They are well on toward completion.

Royal Mint, refinery, buildings and equipment, $57,000.

['I will undertake that information will be furnished to the committee from both my own department and the Militia Department.\nSome resolutions reported.\nMr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House. He said: On Tuesday next I propose to proceed with the Bills representing the French Treaty.']

This amount is for payment upon the refinery which is being erected in connection with the Royal Mint, the construction of which was authorized at the last session of parliament. The total cost of the building of the refinery and equipment is estimated at a little over $60,000. The equipment is quite expensive and consists of very delicate and expensive machinery. It will cost $32,000, including customs duties of $2,000.
Is the building now under construction?
It is partly constructed now, by contract.
Will this complete the building?
The amount of the contract is $31,047.
You had $30,000 voted last year and have spent $10,000, and now ask $57,000, which would make $67,000 if you spent it all.
Instead of $63,000?

I will show my hon. friend how this $67,000 is arrived at. Amount paid for advertising, $358.84; supplies, hardware, repairs to roof and boiler, $205.42; amount of this contract, $31,747; equipment, fitting, machinery, $32,000; sidewalks and grading, $500; superintendence, $1,943; total, $66,754.26, or within $240 odd of the amount that we are asking.
How many men will be employed in this refinery?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid the Minister of Public Works will only be able to deal with the construction of the building. If the hon. gentleman desires information as to the kind of operations which are carried on there and if he will be good enough to state the point on which he desires to be informed I will be very happy to take a note of it and bring the information at another meeting. I could not tell off-hand, but the refinery will not call for many officers. We had hoped to have avoided the necessity of having a refinery at all. We had reason to believe that the refining could be done outside by corporations and we were hoping to save the expense of a refinery, but after carefully inquiring into the matter the mint officials informed us that the material they could get outside was not of sufficient purity for coining purposes and so, reluctantly, we had to undertake the construction of a refinery. I do not understand that it calls for many officials in addition to the present staff, but upon that, as upon any other point in connection with the administration of the mint, if any hon. gentleman will mention the point that he desires information upon I will be very glad to bring it down at another meeting.
Will the minister be good enough to tell us the total cost of the Royal Mint, including the refinery?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is on ' Hansard between $500,000 and $600,000.
I understand the hon. Minister of Public Works now to say that this will cost about $66,000.
The minister first gave the figure as $63,000.
I had not these additional figures in my mind then.
Do you not see how we are misled? We accept that as correct and if the minister afterwards corrects his statement it rather discredits .the information given by him.

I understand that I the present vote is only for the refinery.

What we call the Royal Mint is something different altogether?
This is part of the mint.
What would be the entire cost of the Royal Mint, refinery and everything connected with it? Would it amount to three-quarters of a million?

It is less than three-quarters of a million. The total expenditure on the Royal Mint up to the 31st of March last was $535,238.62. That includes the site. I do not imagine there has been anything expended since that outside of what has been spent on the refinery, amounting to $66,754.26. That will make it a bit over $600,000.
Does the minister remember the original estimate that was given to the House?
No, I do not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was certainly very much below that.
About half.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The original estimate was between $300,000 and $400,000. But, of course, all public buildings have cost more since the time that estimate was made. The work was undertaken on a somewhat broad scale and I am sure the feeling of the hon. gentlemen is that if you are to have a mint you should have a good one. I confess that I was anxious that instructions should be given- that if the mint was to be placed there we should have the most perfect machinery that it was possible to procure, and I believe we have it. I do not know how many hon. gentlemen have had an opportunity of visiting the mint, but if there are any present who have not been there, I think they would find it a very interesting place to go. I believe that every hon. gentleman who has gone to the mint has realized the fact that the work done there is of a very fine character. It was all done by contract and I have reason to believe that it was carefully and well done. I was surprised at the cost myself, but when we were doing an expensive piece of work of this kind we thought we should have it thoroughly well done by scientific men.

I am very glad the minister has extended an invitation to visit the mint. I had it in mind to visit it to-morrow and I was not sure if they would require a letter of introduction from the Minister of Finance in order to get inside to see what was being done.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am sure that any 'member of parliament presenting his card would be welcomed there. It would be a convenience if hon. gentlemen would let them know the day before. I would not

I advise the hon. gentleman to go on Saturday because that is a short day and he might not see as much as he would upon another day. But if any hon. gentleman would telephone any afternoon that he would like to go on the following day, I am sure he would be welcomed and that it would be very interesting.
The hon. gentleman will require more than his card as a member of parliament to get in there. The mint officials require a letter. I found that out myself.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not blame the mint people for being a little more stringent than at ordinary places, but there are a number of instances in which hon. gentlemen have asked me and I have said: Go down and present your card, and I rather think they admitted these hon. gentlemen without question. However, there should be no difficulty on that score. If any hon. gentleman intimates to me the time when he wishes to go to the mint they will be only too glad to have him.
Will the Minister of Finance give an idea of the amount of loss that the country has sustained from the operation of the mint during the last few years?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As the question before the House is merely that of a contract work upon the refinery I did not anticipate questions of that character. I would rather bring in a statement at a later date. I would not care to answer the question from memory.
Is there a residence in connection with this establishment for any of the employees?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. The imperial authorities were very anxious that there should be a residence, but I advised the Minister of Public Works to try and disregard that for the present, and we have no residence. It is the practice in connection with Royal Mints elsewhere that the chief official resides in the mint and there is an advantage in it. However, the building was proving so much more expensive than we had anticipated that I have ventured to take the risk of the displeasure of the imperial authorities up to the present time and have not asked for a residence.
Do you pay the rent of the chief officer's residence in any other part of the city?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think we make an allowance. It is done under the regulations of the Royal Mint and we contribute a lump sum for maintenance and upkeep generally. My recollection is that there is an allowance granted for the residence of the deputy master. .

The hon. gentleman stated that members' of the House could get in on presenting their cards? I presented my card at the mint and I was told I could not be admitted unless I made an appointment a day or two before.
You looked suspicious.

I was also given to understand that the officials were not under the control of this parliament, that they were the appointees of the British government, and that though we had the privilege of paying for the mint we had nothing to say about its engagement. I would like to hear from the Minister of Finance on this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Last session a notice was placed before all members of parliament intimating the times at which it would be most convenient to have them visit the mint, and many hon. gentlemen took advantage of it. I thought they were now sufficiently democratic to admit any gentleman who was a member of the House, although not necessarily at any moment he thought fit to apply, because I fancy that a large number of gentlemen going down there at different times might make it very inconvenient. The mint is something like a bank and it would not be possible to take visitors to the vaults of a bank at all hours of the day. I do not think it unreasonable that the director should be notified a day before of the visit of a number of members of parliament, and if that were done I have no doubt they would be received at once. It is a fact that the control of the mint is under the British government and that is so for reasons which we thought were good. We decided we would have a branch of the Royal Mint in Canada, and one great advantage of that has been that the building has been erected and the machinery installed on the advice and under the supervision of gentlemen who I have no hesitation in saying are the most experienced mint officials in the world. Had the mint been built as a purely Canadian institution we would have had great difficulty in obtaining equal supervision. While it is true that the mint is under the control of the Royal Mint, I have not the slightest doubt that every courtesy would be extended to every member of parliament who wished to visit it, and that far from desiring to put obstacles in their way the director of the mint would be most happy to welcome them. Last session one gentleman opposite came to me and said: I have just visited the mint, and I do wish that every member would visit it, because I had no conception of what an interesting process was carried on there, and I think every member who goes to the
mint will come away proud of it and pleased with it.

The minister states that the advice of the Royal Mint authorities was taken with reference to the machinery. I had the pleasure of visiting that mint and I noticed that about eighty per cent of the machinery was of American manufacture. Can the minister tell us what proportion of the machinery in that mint is of British manufacture, and what. proportion of American manufacture?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Minister of Public Works who has charge of that would be able to give the information, but if it should turn out that all the machinery is American, that does not show that there is anything wrong with the mint, because the American mints are amongst the most modern and best equipped in the world. I am quite sure that the officials of the mint would get the best machinery possible, and in fact we sent them to Philadelphia, to observe the latest process there. I think it is quite possible that the American mints are more modern and better equipped than even the Royal Mint in England.
When does the government intend to proceed with the coinage of gold?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The object of this vote is to complete the refinery, and we cannot coin gold on any extensive iscale until we have a refinery. They are able to do a little refining now on a very small scale, and they have already turned out a few British sovereigns, under .authority which comes to us by virtue of its being a branch of the Royal Mint. Several of our gold mining companies have sent their gold to the mint and British sovereigns have been produced, but to embark on gold coinage generally you must have a refinery. I hope there will be the least possible delay in turning out the gold coins of Canada.
Is it the intention to coin a five dollar Canadian gold piece?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
What is the relationship between the Royal Mint and our Mint?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Royal Mint of England is an imperial institution having branches in several parts of the British empire, and we asked that ours might be treated as a branch of the Royal Mint. One of the reasons which led us to that were it a Canadian mint proper we could not coin the British sovereign. How far our Canadian people will make use of gold coins is a debatable question and a very interesting one, and as we believed it desirable that we should find a market-if I may so express it-for the gold of the Yu-

kon and British Columbia, we thought it desirable that we should have the privilege of coining not only Canadian gold coins but the British sovereign, which is current throughout the world. There are many people who believe that our gold should be kept in our own country as much as possible instead of it being sent to the mints in the United States. In consideration of the privilege of coining the British sovereign we had to relinquish some measure of control. The chief officials have been sent out from England, the appointments are made under the English competitive system; we surrender something of what might be called patronage, and I am bound to say that as a general result it has worked well.
There is no chance for defeated politicians getting in there?
It is hard enough for members to get in.
This refinery is being built for the purpose of refining the gold to turn into coinage?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have to have gold of a certain standard for coinage and this refinery will be for that purpose.

As I understand it a large portion of the gold produced in Canada is minted in the United States at the present time. If we coin our own gold we will have to pay for the gold which comes from our western country, and mint it, and in the end there will be no profit on the process but rather a loss.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We quite anticipate that the gold to be used at the Canadian mint will be the gold of Canada. We will have to purchase it as others have to purchase it. There is a profit in coining bronze coins and a large profit in coining silver but there is no profit in coining gold. You take a given amount of bullion and you convert it into coins and after you have done so it is not worth any more than it was before, so that to that extent there will be a loss on the process of coinage.
Then I cannot understand the wisdom of going to the expense of building a refinery when at present we can receive our gold coinage from the old land without cost.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Wisely or unwisely one of the objects of the Canadian mint was that the gold which my hon. friend says goes from Canada to the United States should be as far as possible kept within Canada. It was claimed that the city of Seattle has been largely built up by the trade of the Yukon country because the miners who produced the gold from our Canadian Yukon, went to Seattle and even to San Francisco with their gold. It was argued by our friends from British Colum-Mr. FIELDING.
bia, with very great force, that if we could induce these miners to come to Vancouver or any other place in Canada, and could provide there a market for their gold, the trade would follow the gold, and we would keep in our own Dominion, particularly in British Columbia, the trade associated with the gold industry. How far that will work out is, like many another economic question, very debatable; but that is one of the reasons why this mint project commended itself very strongly to hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House.
In your arrangement with the British government, is there any limit to the number of British or Canadian coins in gold that you may turn out1

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. The Mint Act provides that any person possessing gold may tender it to the mint and have it converted into British sovereigns at a stated charge, which is fixed in the Act or the regulations. In that we suffer no loss. Indeed, I think there has been a slight profit from the minting of British sovereigns. When we come to mint our own gold coins, there may be a slight loss.
Is there any limit to the number of Canadian coins you may mint?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. That will be determined by the law of supply and demand. We will make as much coinage as the people absorb in their business. When thev cease to absorb it, we shall cease to make it. British gold is not practically current in Canada at all. While it is the standard of our currency in a certain sense, the British sovereign, which is equivalent to $4,861 of our money, is not available for general circulation in Canada, and, excent in the case of a company which for some reason of its own wants these coins made, I do not think we may look for any very general demand for the making of British sovereigns.
I understand that it is the intention of the government to coin a $5 gold piece of Canadian currency?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, $5 and $10, and we are free to make others if we wish.

I would like to ask the minister if he proposes to ta>:e any steps this year to arrange with the banks to get rid of the large amount of American silver coinage circulated throughout Canada, and have the mint coin a great deal more Canadian silver coinage, which he _ says gives considerable profit in the making.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, we have such an arrangement whereby the banks, for a very small commission, I forget the exact amount, undertake to collect the foreign silver and ship it to the United States. In

that way I think there will be a considerable increase in the work of the mint in coining Canadian silver, on which there is a very large profit.
Will the Minister of Finance be good enough to tell us how he expects the miners of the Yukon to bring their gold to Ottawa and do their trading in Ottawa instead of going to Seattle?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not compare Ottawa with Seattle, but I did compare Vancouver with Seattle. I would not expect them to bring their gold to Ottawa, but we have an assay office at Vancouver, and we expect to get Yukon gold there. The question still remains how far the government will go to get the gold. We have to get Canadian gold for the Canadian mint, and if we have to go to the Yukon to get it, we will go,
Are all the officials of the mint given an allowance in lieu of rent, and, if so, are these allowances included in the general allowance for maintenance, or are they kept separate?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My impression is that there is no allowance made for rent to anybody but the Deputy Master of the Mint, and the reason we make that is that we were required by the British government to provide a residence for him in addition to the salary fixed, and as we preferred not to construct a residence for him, we have made him a moderate allowance for rent instead-I cannot remember the exact amount. Under the statute there is a general vote of $75,000 for the maintenance of the mint. We have been trying to keep it down to that, but it is possible that in closing the account we may have to ask parliament to increase that amount.
What are the coins turned out at the mint-gold, silver, copper and other metals?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is proposed to turn out all the coins which Canada requires- the silver coins of the various denominations, the bronze cent, and gold coins of $5, $10 and $20.
Nothing less than $5?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have the right under the Act to make coins corresponding approximately to the British half sovereign, that is, $2.50. Some said that was too small a coin. However, that is a matter of detail.
What of silver?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: 50 cents, 25 cents, 10 cents and 5 cents.
No dollar?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not of silver. We use our dollar note.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, it is intended that any work of that kind should also be done by'the Mint.
Ottawa Victoria Memorial Museum, $260,000.

This building, all members of the committee know, has been under construction for a considerable time. This amount will complete the building with the exception of about $21,000. It will also provide for the fittings, the furniture, and the general equipment. The contract for the building was let some time ago to Mr. George Goodwin of Ottawa for the sum of $950,000. He was the lowest tenderer, and I think it is generally recognized by those who have seen the building that he is doing his work thoroughly and standing up under his contract in the most creditable manner. The chief architect's estimate of the cost of the building was $300,000 higher than Mr. Goodwin's tender, and the next tender was something like $300,000 more than his. Quite a number of tenders were received.
How much has been expended on it up to date?
Up to the 30th of September last $870,494.52.
What will the total cost of the building be?
The total estimated cost under the present contract, including $75,000 for furnishing, heating, wiring, electric fixtures, elevators, &c., is $1,395,000.
Did the contract call for wiring and heating?
No, the contract for these was given to the present contractor of the building.
What is the cost of the wiring?
Including the fixtures, $30,500.
And the heating?
What was the original estimate of the cost?
For the building alone, $1,250,000. And, if the fittings, furniture and everything of that character were added, it would be about $1,500,000.
I quite understand that. Is that the architect's estimate?
His estimate was $1 -250,000.
And the contractor tendered for $950,000. The architect was pretty far out.
The contractor may probably have been out.
He seems to be satisfied.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, he is not.
The next lowest tender was the same as the architect's estimate.
What proportion of the $1,400,000 was not let by tender?
The heating apparatus, the electric wiring, the elevators and the ventilation.
Have they all gone to Mr. Goodwin?
Yes.
How was the price arrived at?
Our own staff went carefully into the matter.
And did Mr. Goodwin accept their estimates?
He did, reluctantly and after a good deal of discussion and negotiation.
He is an experienced contractor?
Yes, and a very reliable contractor.

How does .the hon. minister justify the letting of $450,000 of this work without tender in view of the resolution passed by this House last session that public works should be let by tender? Because we had got a good bargain on a contract, we then proceed to let the balance to this same contractor without tender.

The hon. gentleman must remember that there is still $100,000 of furniture which has not yet been let. What I said was that the heating apparatus, estimated at $38,600; the electric wiring, $30,000; elevators $32,000, and ventilation $27,000-total about $127,600 not $,450,000, as the hon. member said had been let without tender. If I am asked to justify this, I do it on the principle announced last session and I happen to know that my statement then met with the approval of some of the most prominent of hon. gentlemen opposite, men who know Mr. Goodwin, the contractor, who know what a thoroughly honourable, reliable contractor he is,and who were satisfied, as I am satisfied, that he is standing up under a load which means $300,000 less than the work he is doing for the country is fairly worth, $300,000 less than the chief architect, who is a man of large experience, has certi-Mr. PUGSLEY.
fied the work to be worth. Under the practice which has prevailed ever since confederation, upon the certificate of the architect, the contractor for a building may be given the contract for the fittings also. And this is often to the great advantage of the country. I thought that under the circumstances of the present case it was not unreasonable that this work should be given to Mr. Goodwin at reasonable prices as ascertained by the chief architect after careful consideration. I believe that my course in this matter will meet with the approval of the majority of the members of this committee on both sides.

Are we to understand that the minister (Mr. Pugsley) justifies the violation of a resolution of this House by the plea that some man who is honourable gets the benefit of that violation? That is the way I understand it-that, because Mr. Goodwin has the reputation of being an honourable man, the minister is justified in dealing with him in violation of the resolution of this House.
I do not understand that I have violated any resolution of this House.
Is there not a statute which requires all public works of the value of over $5,000 to be put up for public competition?
No, not in the way the hon. gentleman (Mr. Crocket) states it.
There is some statute of that nature. I have not it before me. Did the minister let this work without tender on his own responsibility, or was there an order in council?

There was an order in council authorizing me to take this course. I may say also that the making of that order in council was absolutely within the authority granted by the statute. I would also say that in the completion of a building of this character it is desirable that there should be no conflict beween those who are doing the electric wiring, putting in the heating apparatus and so on, and those engaged in the work of construction, There is, therefore, great advantage in having the work done by one contractor, provided that it is done at fair prices.
Is the system of ventilation of which the minister has spoken operated by means of fans?
Yes.
Do I understand that the contractor is making a loss of $300,000?

I stated that the contractor is doing the work for $300,000 less than the chief architect's estimate of the

cost, and $300,000 less than the next lowest tender, and I believe he is carrying a very heavy load in connection with it. How much he is losing I do not know. Mr. Goodwin belongs to the other side of politics but I give him credit for being too courageous a man and too good a contractor to come to us and cry about conditions which he has accepted. He has not stated to me what his loss is, but I beleive he is, as I have said, carrying a heavy load, and also he is doing his work in a very creditable manner.
Does the minister know whether the contractor is sustaining any loss at all?
I do not. All I know is that the chief architect was of the opinion he could not do the work without sustaining a loss.
What was the reason that the heating apparatus and lighting was not included in the original advertisement for tenders?
Certain practices grew up in the department.
Hear, hear.

And this practice began at a time which my hon. friend from Grenville and Leeds (Mr. Reid) said was the good old time, and it continued more or less until recently. The practice has been changed, and the chief architect has been instructed as far as nossible to let all the work under one contract.
Why was not the policy applied to the construction of the residence we had under discussion this afternoon?
We had two under discussion, one was the departmental building and it will apply to that absolutely.
What about the other?
That was done under the good old Conservative way.
When was the hon. minister converted?
Quite a while ago.
Was any change made in the construction of the building after the contract was let?
The tower was changed, but it was not much of a change.
What did the change amount to?
There was no extra cost and no saving either way. It did not add to the cost or take from it.
If I understand rightly, there was quite a tower, 40 or 50 feet high, which was taken off. Surely that was some saving.
Only the crown was taken off.
When will the building be ready for occupation?
I think in about six or eight months.

The hon. minister says he does not know that the contractor is losing any money at all. I think that usually when a government contractor is about to make a loss on his contract of some two or three hundred thousand dollars, he will make that public; and since this contractor has not done so, my opinion is he is not losing anything. Is the minister still employing' that architect. There is $300,000 difference between the contract and the estimate of the chief architect. Is the minister still employing an architect who will make an estimate $300,000 more than the work will actually cost, according to the tender accepted? It seems to me that this was pretty wide of the mark.

My hon. friend surely does not suggest that because a contractor' may have made a mistake in his figuring and tendered at $300,000 less for an expensive building then he ought to have done, that implies that the chief architect had estimated the cost of the building as more than he ought to have done? There were several tenderers, men of the widest experience, some of the most practical and experienced contractors we have, whose figures were very close to the estimate of the chief architect, but some $300,000 higher than the tender of Mr. Goodwin. Had Mr. Goodwin not put in a tender, the government would have given the contract to the next lowest whose figures were very close to those of the chief architect. With regard to the latter, let me say this. Hon. gentlemen opposite have passed criticisms on his estimates. The hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Staples) said that his estimate for the residence of the chief astronomer -would be no doubt doubled when the actual cost of the completed building was ascertained. All I can say is that during the time I have been in the department, I have learned to have the very highest respect for the judgment, care and knowledge possessed by the chief architect. He has been in that position some 25 or 30 years, and has held, and deservedly enjoyed, the confidence of all governments which had charge of the administration of our affairs down to the present. I believe that he carefully safeguards the public interests in every way possible.

The Minister of Public Works appears very anxious to keep reiterating the question I put him a year ago. It is somewhat satisfactory for me to know that it was I who opened over a j^ear ago the discussion that -was settled on the floor

this afternoon. On that occasion the minister was gliding along with his estimates in that smooth manner of which he is past master; and when last year I asked certain questions, he assured us that this building would be constructed for not more than $16,000. I then made the statement that, from our past experience in the case of other public buildings, the cost of which very often doubles the original estimates, we might expect something similar in this case. Let me tell the minister that I think I can verify that statement even tonight. If he will go back to the first discussion on the Grand Trunk Pacific, he will find that the right hon. the Prime Minister told this House and the people that its cost would not be more than $13,000,000. What has that public institution cost up to date? Let me ask him what was the original estimated cost of the institution we are now discussing. Was it not about $300,000, and it has now amounted to over '$600,000. You can go through the long list of smaller institutions, post offices, and other public buildings throughout the country, and if the hon. gentleman will take time to look through the Auditor General's Report and compare the actual costs with the original estimates, he will find that in many cases the former has doubled the latter. I hope the minister will now be satisfied and not again bring up my assertion that the cost of the residence of the chief astronomer would be double the original estimate. Let him wait until the residence is completed. Possibly then he will find, if the general reputation of this government for extravagance is lived up to, that I was not very far astray in that statement which I made a year ago. You are not through with the building yet. Next year the minister may listen to what we will have to say when he comes asking for a further amount to complete the construction of that building. I hope the minister will give me a little credit for the statement I made, and I think I would have no difficulty in verifying my statement if I desired to go back and review many of the buildings constructed by this government.
Eastern Departmental Block, revote, $75,000.

This is for the purpose of undertaking a -work which was considered necessary some years ago and which was actually provided for but which the government thought might stand over, even although it was at some inconsiderable inconvenience to the departments which are occupying the Eastern block. The Finance Department particularly is in very great need of additional room. Additional room is required in connection with the Treasury Branch of that department which ought really, in the public interest, to have been provided some years ago. The Justice Department also requires additional room Mr. STAPLES.
and it is very desirable that just as soon as possible the Department of External Affairs should be located in that building. The Minister of Finance reminds me that he is afraid that the room will all be required for the extension of the Finance Department. Still I hoped we might _ be able to have some of the other officials there. The total cost of this extension is estimated by the chief architect at $200,396. The addition will be 120 feet by 64 feet exclusive of the tower, two stories high, with an attic and basement It will contain 31 offices and 8 vaults. This estimate does not include the vault linings, which of course will necessarily cost a considerable sum.
Just before dinner the minister stated it was the intention to place the Department of External Affairs in the new building on Sussex street.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid I will have to put in a word on this subject. I discover that a vote originally designed for the Finance Department is being appropriated to others and I want to warn the Minister of Public Works that until he provides adequate accommodation in that building for the Finance Department I do not want him to allot space to any other. If there is more 'than enough space to accommodate the Finance Department I do not object, but this vote was taken to provide much-needed accommodation in the way of vaults, etc. for the Finance Department ; it has been presented to the House in that way and I wish the Minister of Public Works to have it understood that he is to give only surplus accommodation to any other department.
That is my understanding, the Finance Department is to have first claim on any accommodation constructed.
The minister stated that among other things this is to provide vaults.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

1 suppose that is where he keeps the surplus.
Mr.	FIELDING.	In these growing
times the vaults that keep the surplus have to be enlarged.
Ottawa Public Buildings-instrument testing and standardizing building, Cliff street, revote, lapsed amount, $5,000.
What is a standardizing building?

A small building to be erected on the ordnance lot on Cliff St. for the purpose of standardizing the different instruments, such as surveying instruments, tape and chain measures. It is for

the testing and standardizing of the various instruments used in the Surveyor General's Branch of the Department of the Interior.

My understanding is that the standardizing of weights and measures is done in the Inland Revenue Department, and if they have a building for that purpose it would not seem to be in the interest of economy to establish another building to carry on the same work for the Interior Department.

This is for instruments to be used in the Surveyor General's Branch. The Interior Department send out many surveying parties during the year, and of course it is highly desirable that their instruments should be absolutely correct. If there is such a building in connection with the Inland Revenue Department, I am satisfied it is not sufficiently modern or sufficiently large to meet the demands of the Interior Department, because I have been informed there was formerly a building upon this lot for testing purposes belonging to the Inland Revenue Department. That building was destroyed and I do not think any building has been erected to take its place. The demand for this building has been before the Public Works Department for many years. It has been urged from time to time by the Department of the Interior and it has been represented in the strongest way that there was a necessity for a testing room where engineers can adjust and test their instruments.
How much will the building cost?

The total estimate is $10,000.
Before passing from this item, why should we not pass the item of new departmental buildings and discuss it upon another item,later? This afternoon the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) suggested that we might let the item for the new departmental buildings -stand until the plans had been examined by the committee. But, I would think that it might be better to pass the whole item with the understanding that the matter could be discussed on concurrence.
No, no.
I think there would be a very serious objection because every one of these items requires to be questioned.

Very well; it was only to save time.
Public Buildings, Nova Scotia-Digby public buildings, rewiring, &c., $1,000.
Will $1,000 -complete the work which the minister has in view?
Yes, that will complete the wiring.
What kind of building are you rewiring?

It has been reported that the building at Digby requires to be rewired to make it safe.
Halifax Dominion Building-improvements, repairs, &c., $60,000.
I would suggest that as the members for Halifax are not here, we -might pass over these six items.
I would agree to that if it were a new item, but it is simply to pay the contractor for the work being done on -the building. I will let them discuss it on -any other item.
Perhaps the minister would give us a statement as to the cost and of the nature of the work.
This is to make a payment upon the work of remodelling the whole interior of the Halifax Dominion building. The floors are to be removed, only the walls and roof remaining.
Is it the customs house or post office?

It is the old post office, and we are fitting it up now for post office purposes and for the Assistant Receiver General's office. The customs examining warehouse and the Inland Revenue office were removed to the new customs house building.
How much will it cost?
What is the size of the building?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I cannot give the dimensions, but the hon. gentleman will remember, from his visits to Halifax, that this is the building facing the parliament buildings. It was erected before c-onfedera-ton and is commonly known as the post office building. It was taken over by the Dominion government in an unfinished condition. It was then finished and several of the departments were located in it. The customs house was in one end, the post office in the otheT and half a dozen minor departments upstairs. Gradually it became necessary to hire three or four places in the city and some years ago it was determined to erect a new building right below, or nearer the waterside, for customs purposes. The customs house was removed and temporary accommodation was secured by the post office. This building, which is a very handsome one, is now being reconstructed for post office purposes. Nothing now remains but the walls and

part of the roof. It is really almost a new building. It is intended to be chiefly used for post office purposes, but there will be some space available for others. My own department is hiring quarters in another part of the city, and it is proposed to provide offices for the Assistant Receiver General in this new building. I think there may also be some space remaining for minor offices.
Will it take in the savings bank?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Assistant Receiver
General's office is the savings bank.
I can now give the hon. gentleman the dimensions of this building. It occupies 125 feet on Cheapside and George streets, and 55 feet on Hollis street and Bedford road.

Is it built in a fire proof
manner?
Yes.
Is this the building in reference to which the minister received a report of defective work on the part of the contractor?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, that was the customs house.

Who is the contractor?
Mr. PUGSLEY'. Mr. M. E. Keefe.
What was the contract price?
How does the minister account for the other $50,000?
In addition we require for heating and boilers, $7,500; electric fixtures, without wiring, $1,500; elevators, $8,500; vault lining and doors, $7,000; contingencies and superintendence, $14,150.
Were these matters put up to tender?
Yes.
In all cases?

With the exception of the elevators, for the reason that we make a contract for the Otis-Fensom elevator because we think it-perhaps it is quite a strong thing to say-the only thoroughly safe electric elevator built in Canada.
That is a good advertisement.
It is. If it were not for that we could not justify the letting of the contract without tenders.
Did just one contractor get the work?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
No, not the same contractor.
Halifax Quarantine Station, on Lawlor's island-repairs and renewals, $3,500.
What is, this for?

Repairing the wharf. It was reported in a dangerous condition.
Lunenburg Public Building-improvements,
This is to complete the payment in conxrection with the installation of the clock in the tower and for wiring. The building is to be lighted by electricity.

If an election comes on in Ottawa I would like either to have a new clock put in the< tower ot this building or some very great improvement made in the clock, because it is now impossible to tell the time by it. I think we have a right to expect that the government will take steps to have this clock repaired remembering what they have done in that direction in Waterloo.
I admit the clock is acting very badly and I have taken the necessary steps to have it put in order.
I would also remind the minister that we are very badly in need of a clock in No. 89.
That has been ordered. Mr. HENDERSON. Ordered a year ago.
It wrill be there in a few days, possibly to-morrow, but I do not think so,

Last year I called the attention of the minister to the fact that the cellar of this building got flooded during rainstorms, and that there were some complaints with regard to the quality of the cement wrnrk, and saying that the contract was not being properly carried out.
It must be some other building.
No, it was this building.
I don't remember anything of the kind.
I have it here on ' Hansard.' The minister did not know anything about it last year and he seems to know less now.
Would the hon. gentleman read what is in ' Hansard? '
I will send over ' Hansard' and the hon, gentleman can read it for himself.

Oh yes, I see that the hon. gentleman did make a complaint but I regret that I do not remember making any inquiry about it as I seem to have

promised. My hon. friend did not mention it again during the session and I suppose when the rain stopped there was no further ground for complaint.

I had a complaint before me that the sidewalk was not completed according to contract and the minister led the committee to believe that he would inquire into it.. He now seems to have forgotten all about it.

There has been no complaint in the department and I have asked the chief architect to make a further note with reference to what my hon. friend says.
North Sydney immigration shed, $2,500.
Where will the shed be located?

It is an addition to the Intercolonial railway shed for the accommodation of immigrants.
Parrsboro' public building, $15,000.
Does the department own the site?
We bought it.
What will be the total cost of the building?
We have not the plans but Parrsboro' is quite a nice town, and 1 suppose we would give them a building that would run up to $25,000. It will be for a custom house, post office, &c.
Have you called for tenders?
Not yet.
What did the site cost and from whom was it bought?
It was bought from Mrs. Vickery for $3,000.
What is the size of the lot?
It fronts on Main street, Station street and Spring street, on one street 69 feet, on the other 96, and the other 77 feet.
When will tenders be asked for this work?
During the coming year; as soon as we get the plans ready.
How does it come to front on three streets; I do not understand how that can be unless the block is very small?
It is quite possible that it can front on three streets. You will find a building fronting on three streets in St. John city, and for example the Flat Iron building in New York.
I would like the minister to give the facts about this and not be drawing on his imagination?
Strange as it may seem these are the exact dimensions on the various streets.
I do not see how it can possibly front on three streets unless of course the block is very small.
Why, my dear friend-
Oh!
Oh pardon me. I was going to say that it almost paralyses one to think that my hon. friend does not know that a building could have a frontage on three streets.
They must be very small lots in that town.
What streets will it front on?
On the three streets.
How many sides on the building?
Two, the inside and the outside.
I think the committee should get down to business and have some sensible information from the minister.
Did the hon. gentleman ask me a question?
The minister seems to think this is a great joke.
The minister is the most serious man in the room.
The minister thinks it a great joke to compare this building with a flat iron building or a round iron building or a smooth iron building in New York.	*
Hear, hear.
The Minister of Railways says hear, hear.
No he did not.
Perhaps the minister will now tell us the dimensions of the building on each of these three streets.

The building has not been laid out, but if you take the dimensions you will find that the lot is just of a size upon which you can construct a building suitable for a town of that size and having a frontage on three streets. Of course there may not be an entrance on each of these three streets but it will have a frontage on each.
Which is the main street it will front on?
On the Main street.

I might want to go down there to see this wonderful building



and I do not want to get mixed up looking
for a building something like the flat iron . building in New York which the minister has referred us to for a comparison. The minister ought to be able to give us some description of the building before he asks us for a vote.

I am surprised that an hon. gentleman who is usually so serious should, now when we are dealing with the important question of voting public moneys lapses into frivolities and attempt to disturb the serious calm of this committee.
Shelburne public building, $3,000.
Did the Minister of Finance promise that at the by-election or the general election?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I did not promise it either time.
Wolfville public building, $15,000.
This is to enter into a contract for the erection of a building at Wolfville which is a very rising town.
What will be the total cost?

We have not the plans prepared as yet but I should think this building ought to be erected for $20,000. It is a very nice town and there should be a building which would be creditable to it, but I think $20,000 would cover the cost.

Are we to understand that when the minister gives an estimate of the total cost of these buildings that under the new arrangement, that includes the heating and the lighting and everything pertaining to the building.
Yes, I intend to cover that; I may be astray of course until the details are worked out.
What did the site cost?
What is the total cost including site, and everything else when the building will be ready, for occupation?
I cannot say absolutely but what we have in mind is a building which will cost, including the site, in the vicinity of $25,000.
There was a vote for this building in 1908 and how does it come that although the $900 voted then was not expended he is asking for this sum now?
I explained in the House last year that owing to the state of the revenue a large number of these public works were dropped in the estimates and Wolfville was one of the number.
Will the buildings at Shelburne and Wolfville have clocks and towers?

I have not yet thought of a clock for the Wolfville building but there is one to be provided for Shelburne.
Charlottetown drill hall extension, $4,000.
Is this the total cost?

Yes, for the work we intend doing.
Summerside public building, $5,000.
This is to replace the present slate roof which is in a bad state of repair. This will complete.
Is it the intention to call for tenders for this work?
We have not yet decided as to that, but I think very likely we shall. We shall if the work can be done by tender as well as by day's work.
That is rather indefinite. Surely the minister has a policy as to that.

The policy of the department is to call for tenders as far as possible for all public works, but in some cases we find that certain works, such as repairs to a wharf, can be done more cheaply by day's work than by tender. In some cases we have called for tenders, and the tenders have been higher than the chief architect or the chief engineer has reported to be fair and reasonable, and we have done the work by day's labour and done it for less than the amount of the lowest tender. The present work, I think, we can do by tender, and we intend to ask for tenders.
Public Buildings, New Brunswick-Bathurst public building-repairs and renewals, &c., $1,000.
This amount is to make provision for repairs and renewals and also for a concrete sidewalk along the front and side of the building.

In the New Brunswick items I notice five revotes of amounts previously voted which have now lapsed. May I ask if every vote for the province of New Brunswick which has lapsed is renewed in these items, or has my hon. friend made a selection of some?

I do not remember any items that have been dropped.
Fairville public building-revote of $3,000 lapsed, $15,000.
This is to enable us to enter into a contract for the building. The site was purchased pursuant to a vote passed in 1908.
How much will the building cost?	.
What will it contain?
A post office, and we trust also a savings bank.
Will there be room for a janitor in the building?
Yes.
This is not on three streets?

No, it fronts on the main street. I may say that Fairville is a very important town. The monev paid out in wages alone averages about $450,000 in the year. My hon. friend knows that it is one of the most important manufacturing cities in the Dominion of Canada. It has a large number of mills, a very large pulp industry and other industries, quite a number of important business houses and some fine residences. There is a very thrifty population settled at Fairville and its vicinity, and I think it is well entitled to a public building.

I quite agree with the minister that the town of Fairville is growing and increasing rapidly, and that it is as much entitled to a post office building as other towns of the same size, or towns of even smaller size which are getting them.
Fredericton Dominion public buildinggovernment share of cost of permanent pavements put down by the municipal corporation on Queen and Carleton streets, $2,934.87.
This payment is in accordance with the principle of paying the frontage tax where granolithic sidewalks or asphalt pavements are being constructed by the municipality.
Is this the whole of the government's share of the cost?
It is the whole, as made up by the officials of my department, though there is a little difference between the city and my department. This will be paid to the city.
Is the government's share half the cost?

My understanding is that we shall pay half the cost of the pavement on that side of the street immediately in front of the government building; in other words, one-fourth of the total cost of both sides.
I think the impression in Fredericton is that the government was agreed to pay one-half of the whole cost. I suppose the department has an agreement with the city in the matter?

Yes.
19i
Grand Falls public building-revote of $4,050 lapsed, $15,000.
This will enable us to enter into a contract for construction.
Is that the total estimated cost?
No. The total cost will be $20,000 or $25,000.
Are the plans prepared yet?

Not yet. Grand Falls is a thriving growing town with magnificent water-power, the best east of Niagara, and it is expected that there will be development . of that power very soon. I think that the town is well entitled to a public building, and there is at present no public building in the county of Victoria of which Grand Falls is the shire town.
When the hon. gentleman first introduced this proposed expenditure, he said to the committee that the cost of the building would be only $15,000 or $20,000.

That probably did not include heating and wiring.
Hartland public buildings, $5,000.

I do not object to revotes, but when it comes to a question of voting for the first time public moneys for public buildings in this country, I want to remind the hon. gentleman of a question I brought to his attention last year. That was the necessity for a post office at Lethbridge, not for the purpose of beautifying the city of Lethbridge but of meeting the necessities of the people. Over a year ago I received a communication from the post office authorities stating that relief could only be secured by a public building. My duty, I presume, ends when I draw the attention of the government to that feature. I did that very fully last year. I see that no provision is made for a post office there in the estimates this year. I realize that this country is growng and that it is almost impossible to keep pace with its needs, but at the same time there are instances, this is one, when something must be done. Only to-day I received a letter from a business gentleman in the city of Lethbridge referring to business matters, and he added this postscript:
Can you not impress on the department the necessity of providing a post office here. The congestion is out of all reason.
I suppose the hon. minister is aware of that. I do not know that I could do any more than what I did last year and what I am attempting to do now. I have a question on the Order Paper that wall come up on Monday, and I want to put myself on

record now. When it comes to providing votes for new buildings, I would like the hon. minister to understand that the people in the west will have every opportunity to consider these matters and will hold the government responsible. It is not a question of partyism but merely of meeting the needs of the people in the country.

I may say to my hon. friend that there are not many new votes for nublic buildings in these estimates. I . have endeavoured as far as nossible to implement the pledge which was given parliament two years ago. I said then that the public works which had been provided for previously and which had been left out on the estimates were works which were simply postponed, and that when the turn in the tide came, so far as revenues are concerned, I would ask parliament to revote the amounts in order to enable the Department of Public Works to proceed with these various undertakings except in cases where, on further investigation, I was satisfied that they were not required, or not immediately required in the public interest. I think it will be found that in nearly all cases that promise has been carried out in the estimates now before the committee. The case of Lethbridge is one which certainly appeals to me. I have been very glad to learn of the rapid progress which has been made by that enterprising town; but it will be found, in the estimates on page 60, that three amounts are given for Lethbridge. We are asking for a vote of $10,000 for an armoury, we are asking for a vote of $6,000 for the enlargement of the customs house and Dominion land office and also for a vote of $6,000 for the immigration building.
These are revotes.

I do not care, you are going to have them. It does not seem unreasonable that the question of erecting a post office at Lethbridge might stand over for consideration at the next session of parliament in view of the fact that we are asking for three expenditures on public buildings in that town.

Our view points appear to be different. It is not a question with me of satisfying the people of Lethbridve by distributing some of their taxes within their own boundaries, but a question of supplying the absolute needs of the people. 1 have not raised my voice in this committee with reference to any revote, and I do not propose to do so; but when it comes to new votes I want the fullest information as to the absolute need of this money being spent.

As regards Hartland, it is proposed that this building shall be utilized for a post office and also for an ar-Mr. MAGRATH.
moury. I am inclined to think that Hart-land has grown to be a place of sufficient importance to have a branch customs house there also, which will be accommodated in this building. The militia have been urgently asking for an armoury, and I think I can say that there is just -as much demand, at all events for this building, in the town of Hartland as there is for a post office in the town of Lethbridge. I may say further that there is no other vote foT any other purpose in Hartland, while_ there are votes for three different purposes in the town of Lethbridge.

Perhaps we might as well settle this matter now. Do I understand the hon. minister to say that there is no possibility of anything being placed for a post office in the city of Lethbridge? We have there to-day a population of 15,000. There is no place in the country which is growing so rapidly. It is growing by leaps and bounds, and people have to stand out in the street waiting their turn to get into the post office and everybody is complaining. If it is understood that absolutely nothing is available for a post office in Lethbridge this year, we ought to know it.	-

There is nothing in the estimates for a post office there this year, and I cannot put anything in them now. I am not aware that there will be any supplementary estimates. There may or may not be. On that point, I can give no assurance whatever. All I can say now is that there is no provision for a post office for Lethbridge in the present estimates. I am glad to know that Lethbridge is growing so ranidly, but it has only begun to take on its rapid growth in the last year or two. If it is a place the size my hon. friend says it is-and I have heard from other sources that it is-I recognize that we must very soon provide a post office for that town.
I must call the hon. gentleman to order-for that city.

I am not sure that the principle laid down by the hon. minister for the erection of public buildings is just what it should be. I understand he proposes to complete all the public works that were promised some two years ago before he undertakes any new ones.
No, I did not say that.
Is that not the policy of the hon. gentleman?
No.

I think we were told a year ago that the intention of the government was that where a public building had been promised prior to the time when

the revenues of the country began to fall off and the government was forced to drop a great many public works which they had intended to'prosecute, they would, before putting any new votes on their list, complete what they had promised. Is not that, m fact, the policy of the government?

My hon. friend may have drawn that conclusion from my remarks, but it is possible that he was not here during all the time when I was urging these estimates in committee-because I had to answer a good many questions put by hon. members who were annoyed at certain items being left over last year. I said that, speaking generally-I used that expression advisedly-that would be the policy of the department. But I also said that there would probably be cases in which, on making further investigation, I might be satisfied that there was not the urgent demand in the public interest for the work which I had been led to suppose there was, and that there might be buildings in other cities or towns, other harbour or river works, more urgently required and for which we must provide. But, I repeat, I said that, speaking generally, the public works provided for in the estimates of 1907-8, but which we were obliged to postpone on account of the condition "of the public revenues would be the first taken up.

There is little difference between the minister's recollection and my own on that point. As to my possibly not having been present at the debates on the estimates, I may say that I came here last session on the day of the opening of the House, I left Ottawa after the gun had fired for prorogation, and I had never been out of the city during the entire session and had never missed a day sitting in this House. So, possibly, I may have been present-I think I was present at practically all the discussions that took place with regard to the estimates.
The hon. member (Mr. Henderson) was here pretty often.
Yes, and the minister may find that I shall be here pretty often this session.
