I hope so.

I mink we have a right to arrive fairly at the conclusion that there is practically no difference between my recollection and the minister's recollection of what the policy was. I do not mean to say that there was to be absolutely no exception to the rule. But I would remind the minister that in the estimates prior to the last general election a great many buildings were promised. They were preelection promises.
Oh, no.
The hon. minister knows as well as I do that a great many public buildings were promised throughout this country just prior to the general election.
The hon. member said they were ' pre-election promises.' That would connect one with the other.

Pre-election promises are promises made before an election. I will allow the members of this House to draw their own inferences as to why these promises were made just before the general election. Of course, I do not accuse the minister -I should decidedly refrain from accusing him-of making these promises for any ulterior purpose. But there is the fact-public buildings were promised from one end of this country to the other which this House did not regard as being urgently needed, and the general impression was that they were pre-election promises made for election purposes. These were all buildings that came under the estimates of 1908. Now I mention that it would not be fair, these buildings having been promised prior to the general election, and especially if they were offered for election purposes, to give them the preference over other buildings that are urgently needed, such as the post office in the city of Lethbridge. I do not see why, if a post office had been promised in my county-which it was not-prior to the election and for the purpose of influencing the electorate, but yet not needed, the government should go on and build that public work to the neglect of other places that have not been so fortunate as to get a promise prior to election. All these preelection promises should be dropped, and the minister should start afresh and deal with the needs of each county as if these pre-election promises had not been made. Only so will justice be done to all localities. I hope that on reconsidering the matter, and in considering the supplementary estimates, this idea will be allowed for-because I can inform the minister, we will and are likely to have supplementary estimates. In twenty-two sessions I have never seen a session in which there were no supplementary estimates, and, as I have observed, new work generally appears in the supplementary estimates.
There were not many last year.

That was immediately after the election-no, there were not many, but there were some. As I say, new works generally appear first in the supplementary estimates. No doubt, we should have a recurrence of that this session, though not perhaps to the same extent as in former years. I hope that my hon. friend from Lethbridge (Mr. Magrath) will not

be forgotten when the supplementary estimates are in preparation.
What is to be the total cost of this building?
We hope that it will not exceed $10,000.
I understand that it is to be for post office and armoury. Is it not unusual to build these two together?

It is; but I believe it would be a very good idea to adopt the practice more generally-in towns of this character to have part of the public building used as an armoury in which the arms and stores of the militia are to be safely kept. "
What is the size of the garrison in Hartland?
I do not know, and the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden) is not here at the moment.
Has the minister any idea of the population of this place?
I should say from 1,200 to 1,500. My hon. friend from York (Mr. Crocket) would know.
I should think the minister's estimate is not far astray. What proportion of the cost is assigned to the armoury in the estimates?
It is not divided; it all comes under my department.
I should think the architect could tell us how much the armoury would increase the cost of the building.

We have not the plans prepared. I will be able to give the hon. member that information next year.
Hillsborough - public building-revote of $1,970 lapsed, $15,000.

The site for this building, which is admirably suited for the purpose, has been given free to the Crown by the Hillsborough Manufacturing Company. I have about the same statement to make with regard to this building as with regard to the other; I think this work should be entirely completed, including heating apparatus and fixtures, for something under $20,000.
I suppose this site was given by Mr. Osman in return for the wharf made for the manufacturing company by the Public Works Department.
The wharf?
Yes.
I do not know of any wharf given to the company. My hon.
friend is mistaken. The wharf built there is a public wharf, built for the convenience of the public.

The money was voted and expended for an extension of a wharf which is used exclusively by the Albert Manufacturing Co. That is the information I have in regard to the Pink Rock wharf and that the public derive no benefit from that wharf.

It would be more convenient to discuss the item of the Pink Rock wharf when we come to harbours and rivers. The trouble with my hon. friend is, and I think it is a misfortune for him, that he is all the time thinking of hidden motives and interested motives and improper motives. As far as Mr. Osman, the manager of the Albert Manufacturing Company, is concerned, I say to my hon. friend that he cannot get a man in New Brunswick, outside of himself, to deny it -there is no more honourable, straightforward man in the whole Dominion of Canada than Charles J. Osman. His company is carrying on an enormous manufacturing business whose sales extend throughout the eastern United States and a large part of the Dominion of Canada. As far as this wharf at Pink Rock is concerned, the company gave the right to use 'it to the public and the Crown is extending that wharf for the public convenience and to facilitate a large business in connection with which hundreds of men receive employment in that vicinity ana many thousands of dollars are expended annually. I do not know of any wharf built by the Crown for such a small amount which affords so much convenience or gives such accommodation as the extension of this wharf. As far as the public building is concerned, the comoany were anxious to see a public building erected and they generously gave a site for the purpose.

I understood the minister to state that he did not propose to discuss the subject of the Pink Rock wharf, and then he proceeds to discuss it. My reference to the Pink Rock wharf was simply in connection with the minister's statement that this site for a post office was given so generously by his friend, Mr. Osman. I am not here to make any reflection upon Mr. Osman. It is a favourite method of the minister, whenever a fact is stated which might inure to the detriment of his department, to sound the praises, the high character and great reputation enjoyed by this and that gentleman. The House will remember that in the session of last year he sang the praises of another very distinguished friend of his in New Brunswick as one who enjoyed the highest reputation from end to end of the

Dominion, against whom not one word could be snoken, his bosom friend, George McAvity.
Hear, hear, as honest a man as any in Canada.

The gentleman who got away with the $36,000 rake-off in the Mayes contract, Mr. Mayes being the same gentleman from whom the Minister of Public Works received the $2,000 note which he would have the members of this House believe was received for professional services.
And what does the hon. gentleman insinuate it was received for?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think the discussion is wandering away from the item before the committee. I must ask the hon. member to confine himself to the item before the committee.
The minister has asked a question

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The minister may ask a question which it is not proper to answer, within the rules of the House. I rule that the hon. gentleman is wandering away from the point at issue and ask him to confine his remarks to the item before the committee.

I am simply replying to some observations made by the minister which grew out of this item, and you will remember, Mr. Chairman, how the matter arose. The minister was referring to his friend's great generosity in donating a site as if he were a public benefactor, and in connection with that statement the thought came to me of certain information which had been communicated to me.
I rise to a point of order. The way the matter arose was this. I stated
What is the point of order.

The hon. gentleman has not stated correctly how the matter arose. I stated that this site had been donated by the Albert Manufacturing Company. The hon. gentleman then said: I suppose it was in return for the wharf which the government generously built for Mr. Osman at Pink Rock. That was an insinuation, in my judgment, which is not worthy of an hon. member of this House.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The point is, I think; scarcely a point of order; it is rather one of correction. I will still ask the hon. members to confine themselves to the item before the House. I think I cannot properly allow the discussion to wander to the items the hon. gentleman has been bringing forward.

You will understand that I am speaking solely because of a statement and some reflections that the minister sought to cast on myself. I did not rise to a question of order when he described me as a gentleman always seeking for some hidden motives, which statement,
I think, transgressed the rules of the House; and it was because of that state ment and that statement solely that I rose to reply to the minister. When I referred in connection with this observation of the minister to matters that grew out of the very reference of the minister, then the minister seeks to call me to order.
I did not call the hon. gentleman to order.
But if the minister wishes me to answer his question as to what I suppose and believe he got the $2,000 note for I am prepared to state my belief. I believe the statement of Mr. Mayes.
The hon. gentleman has made the statement to this committee that he believes the statement of Mr Mayes.
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
The statement of Mr. Mayes is false, and the hon. gentleman should take that back, Sir.
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have refused to allow the hon. member for York (Mr. Crocket) to continue the discussion along the lines on which he was proceeding. I must still adhere to that. I did not want to be too abrupt, I could not tell to what extent he desired to go in continuing _ to speak, but the point that is under discussion is the Hillsborough public building. I will not, as far as my power goes, allow the discussion to wander to the items that have been brought forward. It is always impossible, where there has been attack and reply to cut short discussion at a point that will please each hon. gentleman. In that respect I mav not be able to satisfy every one, but I must ask the committee to confine itself entirely to the Hillsborough public building.
Did you hear the hon. gentleman state that he believed the statement of Mr. Mayes?
Order.
A man who either in this House or outside-
Order, order.
I say that Mr. Mayes is a shameless and wicked perjurer.

Order.

Moncton-public building-addition to building and alterations to fittings, $10,000.
Perhaps the minister will explain this?

This is to make an addition to the public building at Moncton, 35 x 27 feet. We are to make some alterations to the fittings, modernizing it. The estimated cost of the addition is $8,500; alter ations to the fittings, $600; contingencies-and superintendence, $900, total, $10,000. We expect this amount will finish the improvements to the building.
St. John drill hall, $35,000.	___
Perhaps the minister will explain this item.

It is intended to erect a drill hall in St. John, and for that purpose the Crown has expropriated a site which I think is admirably adapted for the purpose, on Sheffield street, between Wentworth and Sydney streets, taking in two blocks near the exhibition grounds. Although we have expropriated the land, we have not yet made the payments to the owners because they have not agreed to take the amount which has been offered, and it is possible we may have to place the matter before the Exchequer Court, although I trust that an amicable arrangement will be made. We had a small appropriation last year which will -be available foT the payment of the land up to the 31st of next March, and with the vote we are asking for now we will be able to have the tenders called for and a contract for the erection of the drill hall entered into. For a good many years there has been a recognized necessity for a drill hall at St. John. The present one is quite old. It is a wooden building and it is not at all well adapted for the purposes of the militia. I think I can safely assure the committee that this work is absolutely required in the interests of the militia and the public.
From the minister's statement, I judge that the plans of this drill hall have been already prepared. Is that correct?

Plans were prepared some years ago, but we have not prepared new plans for a building upon this site. It may be that there will be some change necessary. Possibly some slight alterations in the old plans will be all that will be required. We could not prepare the new plans until we got the requisite vote for the purpose.
What is to be the size of the building? Has the minister any details at all?	I

I cannot tell my hon. friend at present. We have a memorandum from the Department of Militia as to what they require, but we have not yet decided to erect a building according to the requirements of the Militia Department. However the Militia Department suggests a building 199 feet by 124, with two wings at the rear, each 40 feet square. They ask that the drill hall shall be 193 iby 80. There will be two wings upon the building according to the suggestion of the Department of Militia, and it will be two stories with a 'basement. It will contain armouries for eight companies of infantry. It will also have a gun shed, wagon shed, harness room, and armouries for the garrison artillery, army service corps and bearer company. Whether we can meet the views of the Militia Department entirely, I am not prepared to say. The estimated cost of a building such as the Militia Department ask for would be about $200,000. Whether we can afford to erect a building of that high character or not, I am not prepared at the moment to say.
Could the minister give any idea when these plans will be available so that they can be seen? Have any orders been given yet to make the plans?

I could not have the plans made until the estimate had passed parliament. Just how soon the plans will be ready will depend on how soon the estimates go through; I presume some time during the spring or summer.
I take it that this item is just to pay for the land expropriated?
No, to do more than that. I rather hope that we will get the land paid for out of the money which we have available during the current year.
That is only $2,500.
We have $12,500, and we hope that $10,000 will pretty well pay for the land.

There have been a great many of these buildings before the committee to-night, and it struck me as strange that the minister has never produced a plan. It would facilitate matters very much if plans of proposed buildings were laid before the committee.

I am asking in these estimates for 1,200 different works. If I brought down 1,200 different plans of public buildings and wharfs they would fill this whole room and nobody would look at them. If there is any plan which my hon. friend desires to see, or any information he wishes, I will be very glad to give him a note to the chief architect and he can go and look the plan over. Plans have never been

brought to the committee unless specially asked for in some particular case.
I would like to ask the hon. gentleman to bring down a plan of the building that fronts on those three streets that we inquired about a little while ago.
As soon as that plan is ready I will be very happy to do so.

There is another duty devolving upon the minister which he has not yet fulfilled. He is proposing to undertake the erection of a building which he says, according to the judgment of the Militia Department, will cost $200,000. He asks a vote for that. Whether he has or has no plans it seems to me that an intelligent business department would reach some understanding as to what they intended to build and as to about how much it is going to cost and let the House know what that cost is going to be before we vote any money to commence the undertaking. We want to know what we are committing ourselves to, the size of the building, whether there is a need of the building or not, whether what the people ask for is more than they should get and what the government have decided that they are prepared to do in supplying the needs of the people in that place. In other words give us all the information we ought to have to enable us to decide whether we ought to vote that money or refuse to vote it. We ought to know what we are committing ourselves to because afterwards we are confronted with the arguments that we ought to have taken our objection to it when the vote was asked and before the money was spent. Now we are committed to it, contracts have been let and ,we are obliged to vote the money if we think it wise or not. We want the information at the proper time, and this seems to be the proper time to get the information with regard to this item.

We have to be governed in my department very largely by what, in so far as drill halls and armouries are concerned, are the requirements of the Militia Department. My hon. friend can see that it would not be wise to erect a drill hall which, when it was completed, -would not give the accommodation required for the militia.
It is on the basis of that information that council decides whether it is wise or unwise to put that item in the estimates.

As far as St. John is concerned, it was decided years ago to give them a new drill hall. I think it was decided ten or fifteen years ago, when the old government was in power. I think it has been the view of the different ministers that when a new drill hall should be erected in the city of St. John, it should be one that would be creditable to the city and the country and would give the militia the requisite accommodation. St. John is a very important city, having a population, with its suburbs, of about 55,000. The military spirit is very strong in St. John. It has a regiment of artillery and one of infantry, and it has been felt by noth officers and men that great injustice has been done to them in not giving them a drill hall long before this. If we can get the cost of the building below $200,000, we will do so, but I cannot hold out to the committee any expectation that the cost will be less. If it costs that much, it will not be as expensive as the drill hall at Halifax or the one at Hamilton, not nearly as expensive as the one it is proposed to erect in the city of Toronto, and I doubt if it will be very much more expensive than the one erected in the city of Sherbrooke. Nobody will say that $200,000 for a drill hall and armoury in a city of -the size and importance of St. John is an excessive amount, provided it is built substantially of brick and stone and fireproof material, and we do propose that it shall be constructed in a very substantial manner.

A good deal of what the minister has said is outside of the question altogether. I was not arguing that St. John was not entitled to a drill hall or whether it was costing too little or too much. I was arguing that when the minister submits an item for a new building or a new work of any kind, he should have some data to submit to parliament showing how his estimate was arrived at. I think he ought to tell us what data he placed before Council.

I have told my hon. friend that the Militia Department has asked my department to provide a drill hall and armoury of a size which my_chief architect estimates will cost $200,000. Until the architect prepares his plans and details I am not prepared to say positively whether or not we can provide a suitable building for less. All I can say is that I do not believe the cost will exceed $200,000. If I can save anything on that, I will do so.

I may say that this matter of a drill hall for St. John has been be-for parliament on several occasions and items have been frequently placed in the estimates for it. I think that in the very first year that I came here I found an item for it in the estimates. So far nothing has materialized, and yet there is no place in the whole Dominion that needs a drill hall more than St. John. I believe that the old drill shed there now was about the first one built in Canada. It is of wood and in wet weather one cannot keep dry in it without an umbrella. The garrison there con-

sists of a regiment of artillery and a regiment of infantry besides tne Army Service corps and the Army Medical corps and we have also to house the heavy 4.7 guns which require a good deal of room. When a drill hall and armoury is to be built there, it would be very foolish to build it of anything but brick and stone. The armoury at Halifax cost from $500,000 to $750,000. In St. John we are not looking so much for extravagant expenditure as for the erection of a really needed armoury and drill hall; and comparing the cost of similar buildings in various parts of the country, members of this House will hardly expect to get anything there worthy of the name and suitable for the requirements at anything less than $200,000.	.
St. John quarantine station, Partridge island-water service and improvements, and repairs to buildings, &c., $2,500.

There is great complaint from the Water and Sewerage Board of the city of St. John of the great wastage from leaky pipes carrying water from the west side of the harbour to Partridge Island, and in connection with this I will read a short item which I have taken from one of the St. John papers:
Improvement needed.-Residents of Lancaster and Carleton Heights complain of the frequent scarcity of water. Carleton water officials say that the great trouble is the enormous leakage through the pipes to Partridge island.
This leakage, which has existed for some time, grows constantly greater despite all efforts to check it. According to dwellers on the heights, the scarcity of water is often a very great inconvenience, and the condition is such that vigorous efforts should he made to meet the conditions.
This is a statement made in the press. And -certainly statements are current that there is a very great leakage from this pipe adjoining the service in St. John West with Partridge island. The pipe is under water, and it may be difficult to find the leak, nevertheless there should be some way of finding it and stopping it.

Whereabouts is the meter situated-on the Carleton side or on the Mr. DANIEL.
island side? In other words, who is paying for the leakage,-the government or the city of St. John?	.
The chief architect is not quite sure, he tells me. He thinks that recently one was placed on the Carleton side, and if that was done, I suppose it wias to make the department pay for the waste.
That is the way it ought to be.
I do not think so.

As a citizen of St. John, I would like to know whether the city is or is not paying for the leakage due to the officials of the Department of Public Works not attending to this matter. It must be quite a large amount in the run of a year, and I would like to know
The department is a very good customer of the city for water.
Not very good. Where is the meter?
I shall have to find that out. The chief architect says it was formerly on Partridge island, but he thinks that latterly one was put over on the Carleton side.
Will the hon. minister get that information?
Not to-night.
When?

On Monday, probably.
St. John quarantine station, Partridge island-to provide for full and final settlement of contractor George McArthur's claims for works performed, &e., in connection with his contract of 26th August, 1904, for the erection of two detention buildings and a hospital, $301.80.
Is that the full amount of the claim?

I think so. At all
events, it is all I am prepared to recommend.
Tracadie Lazaretto-house and barn, &e., $3,000.

This is a residence and barn for the doctor at the Tracadie Lazaretto. It is urgently asked for by the medical superintendent.
Public AYorks - chargeable to income- Maritime provinces generally - Dominion public buildings - renewals, improvements, repairs, &c., $15,000.
Is that the same amount as last year?

Yes. There is one other item that, I am sure, the committee will

pass without hesitation. I refer to the item in the supplementary estimates.
Ottawa Military Stores building-to make good the damage caused by fire, $20,000.
This is necessary in order to enable the department to go on with the work.
How did the fire occur?
So far as we can judge it must have been caused by electric wiring getting in contact with some inflammable material.
In what part of the building did the fire start?
The upper part.
Was there [DOT] any insurance on the property?
No, the government is its own insurer.
Are the government buildings all liable to be burned down through defective wiring?
I do not know just what the question means. Fires are liable to occur at any moment.
They are not liable to occur from the wiring if that wiring is put in properly insulated. I ask if public buildings are liable to be burned down because of defective wiring?
I think there ought to be very little risk, but there is a risk. The insulation may be removed from a wire.
Is there no supervision or regulation?
Yes, the experts inspect it.
What do they know about it?
Whatever experts know.

What is that?
Mr. PUGSLEY Well, for one thing, that if the wire is properly insulated and properly installed, the danger of fire from the wires is reduced to a minimum. But sometimes, I believe, the insulation may be removed. For instance a rat may gnaw off the insulating material.

I see by the press that the inspector of one of the insurance companies, looking over many Canadian buildings recently, declared that there was but a very small percentage of them wired in a reasonably safe manner, while many were very dangerously wired and liable to fire, and showing that it was of great importance that some inspector should look over
these buildings and determine whether the wiring had been done properly or not. Has the government assigned that duty to any person? Have they been in the habit of examining these buildings to see whether they are correctly wired or whether the method of wiring may give rise to danger?

When government buildings are being erected, we have an electrical expert who examines very carefully the wiring to see that it is properly insulated, and from time to time we have the electric wiring inspected. In the items we have passed here are some amounts for rewiring which is the result of examination. Some years ago there was not the same care taken with respect to insulating wires which is taken to-day. Electric wiring is much safer to-day than it was some years ago, because greater care is taken to insulate the wires.
When was this building last examined as regards the safety of the wiring and how frequently do these inspections take place?
The chief architect informs me that they are inspected very frequently. I cannot say from week to week or from month to month, but from time to time inspection is made.
Is any record taken when these inspections are made?
I cannot say to-night when the last inspection was made?
When was the building last examined for rats? '

My hon. friend makes a joke of the rat question, but it is more serious than he imagines. I think that rats and mice are responsible for more fires than people give them credit for, in the friction of matches and the destroying of the insulation of wire.	[DOT]
Did the hon. gentleman have any investigation made to ascertain what was really the cause of this fire?

The Militia Department did, but my hon. friend will see how difficult it must be to ascertain just how the fire occurred, provided it resulted from the wiring, and we are not able to trace it to any other cause. If it resulted from the wiring, that is in a part of the building which was destroyed, and it will be impossible to ascertain with what the electric wires came in contact.
What is the total amount of the loss?

If the hon. minister would do what any ordinary company , would do, which had to pay that amount

of money, he would not be satisfied to guess at the cause of the fire. No insurance company would pay out that amount and content itself with guessing whether the fire was caused by rats or mice as the hon. gentleman does.

The building was occupied by the Militia Department and was known as the militia stores building. I understand that the Militia Department made an investigation, but I am not in a position to say what has been the result, and the Minister of Militia is not here to give it.
Then the hon. gentleman should not ask us to pass that item without such information.
We must repair the building at once. It w-ould be the greatest folly not to do so. We must have a roof put on to prevent the rain coming in and destroying valuable property.
But we want the repairs done in such a way that the building will not burn down within another week or two.

My hon. friend need have no fears with regard to the electric wiring, because now that is carried in steel conduits. I would be very glad to give all the information on this subject and will get it from the Department of Militia and lay it before the House, but I would ask the committee to pass the item so that we may get to work with the least possible delay.
Does the minister say that the government carry no insurance on the property but insure it themselves. What kind of insurance is that?

Of course there is no policy issued, but owing to the large number of buildings owned by the government it has always been thought less expensive not to insure at all, because the losses would not be so heavy as the cost of the premiums.
If the government carries no insurance, one would think it would take the ordinary business precaution of having the wiring inspected at regular periods.
If the hon. gentleman means that on a certain day in a certain month each building shall be inspected, there is no periodical inspection of that kind,, but there is a continual inspection going on.
BORDEN, Is any record kept of each inspection?

I cannot say to-night, but I can find out from the expert who Mr. LANCASTER.
does the inspection, and will be able to inform the House later at what time this building was last inspected and what is the system of inspection.
I would think that he should wait until he is prepared to give that information.
In the meantime a big rain might come on and destroy a lot of valuable property.
Or a big rat. It seems to me that the Dominion government should at least take the ordinary precaution exercised by a business firm-
So it does.

I think it should either insure its own property or take steps to guard more effectively against loss. This particular item does not amount to very much, but if all the property of the Dominion, under control of the Public Works Department, is not subjected to periodical inspection, that seems to me a very startling condition of affairs.
Has there been any other fire in any other public building in this city during the last year?
I recall one slight fire.
Caused by a mouse or a rat?
I only know it was put out very quickly.
What fire was that?
We had better pass this item first.

But it is a fair question. We are responsible to the people for these buildings, the people carry their own insurance and we should receive adequate protection, as my hon. friend says, against any fire.

The chief architect says there has been no fire in any of the public buildings except a very slight fire which occurred in my own office some months ago and which was immediately extinguished by means of the hose which was just outside the door. We have a very excellent fire apparatus in the buildings and there was no difficulty on that occasion in putting it out immediately.
In view of the position the item is in, I think it had better stand. The minister says he had no idea the item was coming up.

No, what I said was that I did not know I would be asked the question as to the inspection of the wiring in the buildings and therefore I was not prepared to-night to give the information

as to that. However, I will get the infor mation and will submit it to the committee. I appeal to the good judgment o| the members of the House and ask whether they think that as this building has been so seriously damaged by fire, a building containing a great deal of very valuable property amounting in all to nearly a million dollars in value, which is liable to be injured by rain, the roof having been destroyed, it is in the public interest that this item should be delayed. Should the item not pass in order that we may as soon as possible proceed to the repair of this building?
For what year is it a supplementary estimate?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: For the current year.
The minister spoke of another fire. Has he ascertained what it originated from?
No.
Would it not be advisable to set apart a portion of this money to purchase a rat trap?
The hon. gentleman's suggestions are usually worthy of consideration and very wise and I have no doubt this is as wise as the suggestions he ordinarily makes to the committee.
In view of the intelligence and great prescience of the hon. gentleman from whom it comes, I take it for granted it is accurate.
What will be the total cost of these repairs and will they be done by public tender or day's work?
The total cost is estimated at $20,000 and the intention is to ask for tenders for the work.

I was surprised to hear the minister say that there was so much danger in connection with the wiring of public buildings. He admitted later on that a building could be wired and made . perfectly safe. Every one who knows anything about the system of wiring a building knows that it is possible to wire it so that no mouse or rat can injure the wiring. I think that every public building in this city should be examined and that the wiring in many of them should be changed. A few years ago a serious fire occurred in the Marine Department and many very valuable documents were lost. That fire was attributed to bad wiring. Where it is an admitted fact that a building can be wired in such a way that accidents become almost impossible, every public building in Ottawa should be rewired. I think it would pay the government. Here is a loss of $150,000, an amount which would more than wire every government building in the city and make them perfectly safe. I think that is worthy of consideration.
I quite agree that that is worthy of consideration. Of course when these buildings were erected the modern system of electric wiring was not in use. The new wing has the steel conduits.
I think the information' asked for this afternoon should be brought down later on. We should also have information as to whether or not there was any watchman in that building.
The Dominion Police have charge of the building.
I saw the statement, I do not know what reliance is to be placed on it, that if a watchman or caretaker had been in charge very little damage would have been done.

I will undertake that information will be furnished to the committee from both my own department and the Militia Department.
Some resolutions reported.
